papers.title: Sinkhole susceptibility and genesis at the southwestern slope of the Mount Sirino (Basilicata, Southern Italy): insights from field survey and machine learning modeling
papers.source: Rendiconti online della Società Geologica Italiana
papers.summary: The southwestern slope of the Mount Sirino (Basilicata, Southern Italy) is characterized by complex geological conditions favouring heterogeneous sinkhole phenomena. The most prominent geomorphological feature is Lake Sirino, formed on a large landslide deposit and frequently affected by piping-related sinkhole phenomena. This study uses an integrated approach combining geological and geomorphological surveys, remote sensing and machine learning modelling to investigate the genetic mechanisms of sinkhole formation at Lake Sirino and its surrounding areas (c. 100 km²). Fieldwork identified ten natural sinkholes, mainly associated with deep-seated piping processes in detrital deposits overlying low-permeability substrate. The Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) algorithm was used to create a susceptibility map of natural sinkholes in the study area. This analysis identified lithology and fault density as the primary predisposing factors. The results highlight that sinkholes development in the Lake Sirino area is controlled by the interaction between high hydraulic gradients, fractured zones, and contrasting permeability layers.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility and Runout Modelling Along the Karakoram Highway Using PS-InSAR and Hybrid CNN-LSTM–XGBoost
papers.summary: The Karakoram Highway (KKH) traverses a tectonically active and climatically sensitive mountain corridor that is repeatedly affected by landslides. This study develops an integrated hybrid framework combining convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) learning, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), persistent-scatterer interferometric synthetic aperture radar (PS-InSAR), runout modelling, climate projections, and multi-hazard risk assessment along a 320-km section of the KKH in northwestern Pakistan. Eighteen topographic, hydrological, geological, climatic, anthropogenic, and geodetic conditioning factors were used. The CNN-LSTM was pre-trained on the NASA Cooperative Open Online Landslide Repository and fine-tuned using an inventory of 612 landslides, while class imbalance was addressed using SMOTE and focal loss. The stacked hybrid model achieved an AUC of 0.974, accuracy of 0.928, and Cohen’s κ of 0.856, outperforming standalone CNN-LSTM (AUC = 0.951) and XGBoost (AUC = 0.938) models. SHAP and Grad-CAM analyses identified slope, PS-InSAR line-of-sight velocity, annual rainfall, and elevation as the dominant controls. Flow-R and RAMMS simulations reproduced representative runout patterns with κ = 0.74. Under CMIP6 SSP5-8.5, high-to-very-high susceptibility is projected to increase from 24.0% at baseline to 35.2% by 2050 and 41.6% by 2100. The multi-hazard assessment further indicates that 23.7% of the highway lies within high-to-very-high composite risk zones. The framework provides an explainable, climate-sensitive, and operationally transferable basis for landslide-risk reduction along high-relief transport corridors.

papers.title: Seismic–Tectonic Predictors of Landslide Susceptibility in the Western Himalayas: A Spatially Validated Machine Learning Assessment
papers.summary: Seismicity may contribute to regional slope instability in the Western Himalayas, but its incremental predictive value relative to a matched non-seismic baseline remains poorly quantified. This study assessed the regional contribution of seismic–tectonic predictors using 763 geocoded NASA Global Landslide Catalog reports from 2007–2017, 345 earthquakes of magnitude 5.5–7.6 from 1965–2016, mapped active faults, and hydrographic variables. Landslides were aggregated to a 0.25° grid, yielding 231 presence cells among 1,600 cells. Spatial block-permutation tests, nested five-fold spatial cross-validation, four classifiers, matched baseline comparisons, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were applied. Landslide-presence cells were closer to catalogued earthquakes than background cells (61.5 vs. 118.3 km; P = 0.0005) and had a higher energy-weighted seismicity index (2.323 vs. 2.003; P = 0.0015). Random forest achieved the strongest mean discrimination and calibration (ROC–AUC = 0.855 ± 0.027; PR–AUC = 0.489 ± 0.073; Brier score = 0.096 ± 0.004). Adding seismic–tectonic predictors increased random-forest ROC–AUC by 0.048 and reduced the Brier score by 0.014, although paired tests across five folds did not reach P < 0.05. The high and very high susceptibility classes occupied 16.5% of grid cells and contained 68.2% of catalogued events. Earthquake proximity, Gaussian earthquake density, and energy-weighted seismicity were the leading physical seismic predictors in SHAP analysis. These findings indicate useful regional seismic–tectonic predictive information but do not establish earthquake triggering or causation. Interpretation is limited by catalogue reporting bias, coarse mapping units, mixed magnitude scales, and unavailable terrain variables.

papers.title: From local hazards to connected climate risk: Compound extremes reveal a systemic blind spot
Between emergency and reconstruction: Territorial impacts and climate adaptation challenges after hurricane John in Guerrero
papers.summary: This chapter analyses the territorial, human, and socioeconomic impacts caused by Hurricane John (2024) in the state of Guerrero, with a particular focus on the municipalities of Acapulco and Coyuca de Benítez, within a context of increasing intensity and frequency of extreme hydrometeorological events. Using a territorial and comparative approach, the chapter examines the meteorological characteristics of the event, patterns of differentiated impacts, and the structural vulnerability conditions that shaped the magnitude of damage. The findings show that although Hurricane John exhibited lower wind intensity than previous events such as Hurricane Otis (2023), its extraordinary rainfall produced widespread impacts, including flooding, landslides, and significant socioeconomic disruptions, especially in rural and peri-urban areas. Furthermore, the assessment of post-disaster recovery processes reveals persistent structural gaps related to socioeconomic inequality, fragile urban infrastructure, and the limited integration of climate adaptation criteria into territorial planning. Overall, the chapter highlights the urgent need to move toward risk management and resilient reconstruction models that incorporate preventive, participatory, and territorially differentiated approaches, aimed at reducing future exposure and strengthening community adaptive capacity in the face of increasingly extreme climate scenarios.

papers.title: Uzaktan Algılama ve Yapay Zekâ Entegrasyonu ile Afetlerin Analizi
papers.summary: "Monitoring and managing natural and human-induced disasters is vital for mitigating disaster risks and impacts due to increasing global climate variability, population growth, and rapid urbanization. Disasters such as earthquakes, landslides, and forest fires cause severe damage to human life and the natural environment. Their ability to spread over large areas and evolve rapidly often renders conventional field observation methods inadequate. In this context, remote sensing technologies offer significant advantages for disaster monitoring and analysis due to their capability to cover vast spatial areas and provide periodic data. Multispectral and high-resolution data obtained from satellite systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, and LiDAR technologies are effectively utilized for disaster detection, damage assessment, monitoring spatial-temporal dynamics, and the generation of risk maps. Furthermore, the increasing volume and complexity of remote sensing data have accelerated the integration of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning and machine learning methods, into data analysis workflows. Convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory, and recently developed transformer-based models offer advanced solutions for the automated detection, classification, and mapping of disasters from remotely sensed data. Through the integration of these technologies, applications such as post-earthquake damage assessment, landslide susceptibility mapping, early detection and monitoring of forest fires, and mucilage formation detection can be performed rapidly and effectively. The convergence of remote sensing and artificial intelligence, commonly referred to as Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI), further facilitates the development of risk prediction and decision support systems for potential disasters. This study provides a comprehensive review of the applications of these technologies across different types of disasters, highli

papers.title: Yıkıntı Atıklarının Yönetiminde Saha Değerlendirmesi ve Önceliklendirme Yaklaşımı
papers.summary: "Natural disasters have the potential to generate large amounts of debris. The amount of waste generated in an instant can far exceed the amount that would have accumulated over years, overwhelming local waste management facilities beyond their capacity. This waste leads to deterioration of water and air quality, noise pollution, negative impacts on flora and fauna, visual pollution, and negative socioeconomic effects. If managed effectively, disaster waste can become a valuable resource in the recycling and reconstruction process, contributing to social and economic improvement. Following the two earthquakes on February 6, 2023, with epicenters in Pazarcık and Elbistan (Kahramanmaraş), field visits and various meetings with relevant institutions were conducted in Kahramanmaraş and Hatay provinces to support the development of disaster/waste management plans, and the data obtained was evaluated. Within the scope of this evaluation, the existing dumping sites in both provinces were also examined separately regarding the storage and recycling of demolition waste that is currently present and may be generated from future demolitions. These examinations, along with criteria such as dumping site area, distance to the nearest settlement, distance to pasture land, distance to forest land, distance to a stream, presence of landslide risk, topographical condition of the site, quality, geological structure, and vegetation, were used to prioritize the sites using a multicriteria decision-making method. As a result of the study, an alternative model was developed that can be used to determine the most suitable sites for the storage and recycling of demolition waste."

papers.title: Enerji Altyapılarının İklim Kaynaklı Afetlere Karşı Dayanıklılığı
papers.summary: "This study examines the vulnerability and resilience of energy infrastructures to climate changeinduced disasters from the perspectives of energy security, supply continuity, disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation. It addresses, within an integrated framework, the impacts of major climate hazards such as extreme heat, drought, heavy precipitation and flooding, storms, landslides, wildfires and icing on the energy system. In this context, the study evaluates heat stress and cooling-water constraints in thermal power plants, drought and changes in flow regimes in hydropower plants, temperature-related efficiency losses and site damage in solar power plants, and storm, icing and automatic shutdown mechanisms in wind power plants. It also discusses the risks posed by extreme heat, wind, floods and wildfires to transmission and distribution grids, as well as the climate-related impacts on natural gas, oil and storage infrastructures. The study shows that climate risks do not only cause physical damage, but also disrupt the functioning of the energy system through efficiency losses, capacity reductions, operational interruptions, supply chain disruptions, access constraints and service continuity problems. Therefore, location-based mapping of climate-related vulnerabilities and risks at the level of neighbourhoods, streets, facilities, line routes and critical infrastructure points is essential for identifying which infrastructure assets are exposed to which hazards and to what extent. In addition, institutionalizing data sharing through the protocols envisaged under Climate Law No. 7552 will enable reliable risk monitoring, systematic measurement of vulnerabilities and the timely prioritization of resilience investments. In light of Türkiye’s energy system characteristics and climate policy documents, the study identifies priority areas of sensitivity and develops resilienceoriented policy recommendations, including the updating of design standards, strengthenin

papers.title: Edukasi dan Sosialisasi Kebencanaan Longsor Berbasis Komunitas untuk Penguatan Kelembagaan Komunitas Peduli Lingkungan Kampung Asbaken
papers.summary: Kampung Asbaken in Distrik Makbon, Kabupaten Sorong, faces recurring landslide risks due to steep topography, high rainfall, uncontrolled land clearing, and sparse deep-rooted vegetation. Compounding this vulnerability, local disaster literacy is limited, and the partner group, Komunitas Peduli Lingkungan Kampung Asbaken, lacks formal organizational structures and standard operating procedures (SOPs). This community engagement initiative aimed to enhance community-based landslide mitigation and strengthen local institutional capacity through training, participatory risk mapping, slope bioengineering, and evacuation-route marking. Involving 25 partner members and 30 residents across three workshops, the program evaluated knowledge gains using a 30-item pretest-posttest instrument. The mean knowledge score increased by 78.6%, rising from 48.7 (SD = 9.8) to 87.0 (SD = 6.9), while passing rates (score ≥ 70) improved from 20.0% to 90.0% (paired t = 17.4, p < .001). The partner group also formalized its organizational structure and mitigation SOPs. These results show that participatory education integrated with vegetative conservation and institutional capacity building effectively enhances rural disaster resilience.

papers.title: Integrated subsurface screening for bioengineering suitability and erosion control on a tropical cut slope
papers.summary: Tropical cut slopes are highly susceptible to erosion and shallow landslides because intense rainfall interacts with deeply weathered residual soils, yet bioengineering interventions are frequently designed without adequate subsurface characterization. This study aimed to conduct an integrated geological, geophysical, and geotechnical characterization of a tropical cut slope on the Kenny Hill Formation, Selangor, Malaysia, in order to evaluate its suitability for bioengineering. Field reconnaissance and weathering grade classification were combined with a two-dimensional electrical resistivity survey, soil penetration resistance, near surface moisture content, and erosion rate measurements collected across three vegetation coverage plots over 24 months. The slope was classified as Grade III to IV weathered metasedimentary rock with a sandy clay loam surface texture. Resistivity imaging identified a high resistivity, coarse textured near surface layer of 20,000 to 360,000 Ωm at 0 to 5 m depth, overlying a low resistivity, moisture affected zone of 300 to 800 Ωm at 5 to 14.8 m depth. Penetration resistance increased significantly under vegetation cover, reaching 4.4 kPa in the densely vegetated plot compared with 2.9 kPa in the control, while near surface moisture content and hydraulic conductivity rose progressively and erosion rate declined by up to 74.04% relative to the initial condition. These results indicate that the near surface zone provides mechanically, hydrologically, and ecologically favourable conditions for root establishment, whereas the deeper zone offers limited support for root anchorage. The corresponding reduction in erosion rate confirms that the subsurface conditions identified through this integrated approach translate into measurable improvement in slope performance. Overall, combining weathering grade classification, resistivity zonation, and penetration resistance testing provides a reliable, field deployable framework for screening tropical

papers.title: Shear Strength of Unsaturated Organic Clay across Natural Dry-Density Gradients from Landslide Sites in Bogor, Indonesia
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides in tropical regions are closely linked to the loss of apparent cohesion as unsaturated soils approach saturation. This study examines how the apparent cohesion (c′) and internal friction angle (φ′) of unsaturated organic clay respond to variations in natural dry density (γd) across a range of degrees of saturation (Sr), using natural dry density values obtained from three actual landslide sites in Bogor, Indonesia, rather than from laboratory-compacted specimens. A total of 231 direct shear tests (3 sites × 7 specimens × 3 normal-stress levels × 3–4 repetitions) and 42 filter-paper tests (3 sites × 7 specimens × 2 repetitions) were performed on remolded specimens reconstituted to in-situ γd values at seven Sr levels. The results reveal four main findings. The three soils have very low and uniform air-entry values (1.52–2.09 kPa), so the suction contribution is lost soon after infiltration. Apparent cohesion does not decrease monotonically but peaks at intermediate saturation (44–56%), with peak values tiered according to density (10.60; 6.30; 4.69 kPa). c′ and φ′ respond to Sr through different mechanisms: c′ peaks while φ′ decreases monotonically. The cohesion advantage of the densest soil, prominent under moist conditions, vanishes near saturation, where the cohesion of the three densities converges to a nearly identical low value. A multiple linear regression model, c′ = 16.162·γd − 0.089·Sr − 5.076, is proposed as a practical estimator. These findings imply that initial density alone does not guarantee slope stability under heavy rainfall.

papers.title: 7269 Sayılı Kanun’dan Kaynaklanan Davalarda Genel Durum Analizi
papers.summary: This study examines the scope, fundamental provisions, and legal problems encountered in the implementation of Law No. 7269 on “Precautions to be Taken due to Disaster Affecting Public Life and Assistance to be Provided”, which aims to mitigate the effects of natural disasters and assist victims in Türkiye. Türkiye's location in an active earthquake zone increases the importance of this law. The law covers disaster types such as earthquakes, floods, and landslides, providing a comprehensive framework from pre-disaster measures to post-disaster aid. Among the most frequently encountered legal problems in practice are the criteria and review of disaster-stricken area declarations, appeal processes and judicial review concerning damage assessment reports, property uncertainties and inheritance issues in entitlement determination, value assessment in expropriation processes, and the administration's liability in compensation lawsuits. The annulment decision of the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Türkiye in 2023 regarding the inability of damage assessment reports to be subject to independent litigation is an important development. The study analyses these problems in light of judicial decisions and offers recommendations. Particularly, the necessity of establishing specialised judicial units and adopting effective procedural methods for the swift resolution of post- disaster legal disputes is emphasised. Additionally, the importance of raising disaster awareness and strengthening society's resilience against disasters is emphasised.

papers.title: Landslide-Resilient Hillside Housing: An Integrated System of Biopolymer Soil Treatment, Bio-Engineering, Micropiles and Siphon Drainage
papers.source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.summary: Landslides triggered by rain repeatedly destroy homes and livelihoods on the steep, weathered slopes of the Western Ghats and other high-rainfall hill regions. The usual remedies, retaining walls and deep foundations, tend to be costly, carbonheavy and awkward to build on remote ground, and they are normally applied one at a time even though most slope failures have several causes working together. This paper presents the concept and test plan for an integrated, low-impact housing system that deals with the soil, the slope surface, the foundation and the groundwater together. The soil is strengthened with xanthan gum, a microbial biopolymer that bonds particles and lowers permeability. The surface is protected by vetiver contour hedgerows and bamboo clumps whose roots hold the upper soil. The house stands on micropiles socketed below the potential slip surface, and a French drain with siphon pipes removes the water that raises pore pressure, without pumping. We review the literature behind each component, explain how the weakness of one measure (for example the water sensitivity of the biopolymer) is covered by another, and set out the methodology: site selection, soil characterisation to Indian Standards, a xanthan gum dosage programme, bio-engineering, micropile and drainage design, limit-equilibrium and finite-element stability analysis of four scenarios, and a reduced-scale rainfall model. Expected outcomes are stated qualitatively because no test data exist yet. Materials, a prototype work plan, a maintenance routine and future research needs are also listed.

papers.title: A study on landslide susceptibility mapping by integrating different datasets based on feature and spatial constraints

Sediment reduction or elevated risk? Vertical Heterogeneity in saturated hydraulic conductivity shapes the hydrological trade-off between erosion control and shallow landslide susceptibility on the Loess Plateau
papers.summary: Study region The Chinese Loess Plateau has undergone extensive vegetation restoration, reducing soil erosion but raising concerns about shallow landslide susceptibility under extreme rainfall. Study focus We coupled the Integrated Hydrology Model (InHM) with an infinite-slope stability model in Shejiagou catchment to examine how vegetation-induced changes in saturated hydraulic conductivity ( K sat ) profiles shaped runoff, erosion and stability. Forty vegetation-associated simulations based on measured profile-values together with thirty-two controlled simulations with fixed surface-layer conductivities or average conductivities were conducted. Responses of surface-subsurface hydrological processes, soil erosion and slope stability to the vertical heterogeneity of K sat were compared under high/low rainfall conditions and dry/wet antecedent conditions. New hydrological insights for the region Under high-intensity rainfall on dry soil, profiles with higher near-surface conductivity reduced discharge by 15.8%–68.6% and hydraulic sediment yield by 15.2%–66.6%, yet diverted water was stored at depth and forest profiles developed deeper potential instability than same-age grass profiles, a contrast amplified under wet conditions. Controlled profiles matched in surface conductivity and thickness-weighted mean isolate this mechanism. Altering internal conductivity allocation cut sediment yield by 19.7%–26.7% but enlarged the potentially unstable area from 31.0% to 33.6% and from 45.3% to 53.2%. Erosion-control benefits from vegetation restoration in the Loess Plateau cannot be judged from reductions of runoff and soil erosion alone. Future strategies must jointly weigh erosion control against the increasing depth-dependent potential instability.

papers.title: Socioeconomic and Housing Conditions, Perceived Landslide Hazard, and Stated Adaptive Intentions in Two Hillside Sectors of Quito, Ecuador
papers.summary: Landslides affect low-income households on urban hillsides, yet household-level evidence from Andean cities is scarce. This exploratory cross-sectional study examined how socioeconomic and housing indicators and perceived soil hazard relate to two stated adaptive intentions, willingness to relocate and to modify the dwelling structurally, in two hillside sectors of Quito, Ecuador, with reported landslide events (Pomasqui and Guápulo). Interviewers surveyed a convenience sample of 408 adults, with interviewer teams nested within sectors. Analyses used non-parametric tests, false-discovery-rate correction, and logistic regression. The sectors differed in length of residence, tenure, and housing; 68.0% of Guápulo households, versus 32.6% in Pomasqui, reported no better housing alternative, whereas most risk-perception items differed by less than |r| = 0.20, excluding moderate, not small, differences. Seventy percent were willing to relocate; in an exploratory model with post-hoc pooled hazard categories, willingness was 18 percentage points higher (95% CI 5–31) at low than at medium perceived hazard, but this rested on 54 households (44 in Pomasqui) and a poorly calibrated model. Associations with willingness to modify were borderline and fragile to clustering. Explanatory power was low (optimism-corrected area under the curve ≈ 0.60), and sector was confounded with length of residence. The findings are hypothesis-generating.

papers.title: Rock mass classification in a double bench Quaternary basalt quarry to inform potential high density residential development
papers.summary: For some time, disused and partially rehabilitated quarries in the inner-city suburbs of Australian capital cities have been assessed for potential high-density residential and industrial developments. This trend will increase as major cities continue to grow, while quarry rehabilitation requirements in inner-city areas increase owing to proximity to well-developed areas. Common geohazards associated with redevelopment of quarries are typically either soil or rock mass- governed (pit slope failures) or settlement-related (for example collapse settlement of uncontrolled fill stockpiles). A double-bench quarry up to 25 to 30 m deep in Quaternary-aged Newer Volcanic deposits in Melbourne was assessed for redevelopment, with high-density residential use proposed. A DJI Phantom drone was used to capture nearly 800 photographs and develop a photogrammetry model using Pix4D, for structural interpretation in the Maptek Eureka software package. While drones are now commonly used in field data collection in rock engineering, the use of a drone to capture the photogrammetry model in this instance gave valuable insights into rock mass classification and landslide characterization in Quaternary Basalt, as the elliptical shape of the pit, undulating pit wall aspects, and varying pit bench angles practically reduced biases. When combined with conventional field mapping data, a comprehensive rock mass and structural model was developed to support landslide hazard characterization and assessment of spatial probability in accordance with the Australian Geomechanics Society Practice Note Guidelines for Landslide Risk Management (AGS (2007)). The implications of the assessment for the rehabilitation of Newer Volcanic quarries are discussed, with a focus on safety constraints when working in proximity to blast-damaged benches and durability and maintenance issues associated with most long-term remedial options.

papers.title: Benefits, Costs, and the Size of the Pie: An Economist's Musings
papers.summary: Environmental, health, and safety regulation expands our economic pie beyond GDP. Awareness of accompanying costs motivated BCA in regulatory analysis. Building on Peltzman's (2022) 1973–2018 analysis of public opinion about regulation, I concentrate on confidence in four key institutions and focus on the Obama, first Trump, and Biden Administrations. Included are 2021, 2022, and 2024, the most recent years on the General Social Survey. Confidence patterns are striking. Landslide declines to low levels in both the Executive Branch and Congress are clear. For the Supreme Court and Scientific Community, recent declines are conspicuous, albeit from higher baselines. BCA has likely played a role in sustaining credibility for the Scientific Community in regulatory decision making, at least until 2022 and 2024. The durable 2003 OMB Circular A‐4 Regulatory Analysis became a focal point by distilling consensus methodological practices and standards. But the 2023 Circular A‐4 blurred fundamental analysis of net benefits with mixed analysis that conflated standard WTP with superimposed value judgments. The 2025 Executive Branch transition brought rescission of the disputed 2023 guidance, but contentious deregulatory implementation overshadows BCA now. Essential to enduring economic advice is BCA based on primary analysis of what happens to the size of the pie.

papers.title: Changes and Transitions in Soil Erosion Intensity Classes in Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture
papers.summary: This study assessed how soil erosion extent and intensity changed in Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, southwestern China, between 2000 and 2023. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) was used to estimate soil erosion rates for 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, and 2023. The estimates were grouped into six intensity classes, and a transition matrix was constructed by overlaying the 2000 and 2023 classifications. Very slight and slight erosion together accounted for more than 90% of the classified area in all six years. The area with slight or greater erosion decreased from 15,748.33 km² in 2000 to 15,038.74 km² in 2023 (4.51%), while the area with moderate or greater erosion declined by 12.47%. Erosion extent reached its lowest recorded value in 2010, increased through 2020, and then declined again by 2023. In the endpoint transition matrix, shifts to lower intensity classes accounted for 64.81% of the area that changed class. Class-specific transitions require further verification because the matrix totals by class differ from the annual area estimates. The results support tracking both overall erosion extent and the area in higher intensity classes when assessing regional erosion trends.

papers.title: Shipwreck Coast geohazard management: Loch Ard Blowhole Lookout and limestone arch stability, Victoria, Australia
papers.summary: Recently constructed lookout structures on the Shipwreck Coast are located in actively eroding coastal limestone (karst) terrain and their design needed to consider the probability and consequence of future geological instability. The new lookout at Loch Ard Gorge, situated over the natural limestone arch; replaces the on-grade viewpoint, closed due to geotechnical concerns; and provides much-improved visitor experience. Comprising a central suspended deck substructure, cantilevering on ‘finger beams’ towards the blowhole, and supported on strip foundations set back from the edge, the ends of the lookout are outside the natural arch feature on more competent ground, with a slab on grade substructure. Design considered a number of critical assumptions in context of geohazard risk in the event of sudden large scale ground failure and loss of support to shallow foundations over the natural cavern. The principal assumption being the structure would catenary in such an event and not completely collapse. The design objective was to maximise dramatic views, while minimising risk to visitors and the structures. To understand the balance between maximising view versus reducing risk; sensitivity of position relative to the location of a cliff face was explored using the AGS Guidelines for Landslide Risk Management (2007) methodology. Early assessment considered temporal changes following any cliff failure; that risk will increase as distance to the cliff face decreases. Cliff erosion in this region is both spatially and temporally episodic, at a range of scales. Results for event-triggered (extreme wave-impact / earthquake) cavern collapse (partial and full) scenarios demonstrated societal risk in the acceptable to tolerable range (f–N plot, ANCOLD 2003). Risk to the structure, considering the potential cavern collapse over the design life was shown to be high. Requirements for analysis of arch stability under loads imposed by the structure were identified, (i) a preliminary

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Landslide Susceptibility Assessment and Interpretability Analysis Along the Ningde–Gutian Expressway
papers.summary: This study examines whether high point-based discrimination in machine learning models translates into effective landslide susceptibility zoning along the Ningde–Gutian Expressway, Fujian Province, China. Using 141 historical landslide sites and 12 conditioning factors, we compared SVM, an SVM–random forest ensemble (SVM–RF), XGBoost, and LightGBM. Models were evaluated with ROC/AUC, precision, recall, F1, class-level frequency ratios (FR), and a cumulative success curve; LIME ranked factor contributions. The ensemble models achieved high random-split test AUCs (0.954–0.956), but the available results provided no evidence of a clear performance difference among them. At the map level, only SVM–RF showed a monotonic increase in landslide density from very low to very high susceptibility (0.78–1.46 sites/km2). Frequency ratio analysis revealed weak and partly inverse associations: rainfall was depleted in the wettest classes (FR 0.11–0.64 above 1860 mm) despite ranking first in LIME, and road proximity showed no enrichment (FR ≈ 0.99 within 1 km). These patterns are consistent with LIME importance reflecting spatial confounding and correlated predictors, but they do not prove it. High point-based AUC therefore does not guarantee useful susceptibility zoning; class-level diagnostics and spatial validation are essential. The maps are presented as a screening tool for field verification, not an operational early warning product.

papers.title: Landslide Events, Meghalaya, 2024 to 2025
papers.summary: An online map of 8894 landslide events in Meghalaya, giving each slide's district, location, date and time, type, casualties, 24-hour rainfall, affected highway and status. It is shown with roads and with district and block boundaries. Published on the Meghalaya State GeoHub, which does not name the producer. Event dates run from 2024 to 2025. Detail is one point per landslide. Useful for landslide risk planning and disaster response. Downloads freely from the Meghalaya State GeoHub's public map service, with no sign-in.

papers.title: Validation of a 3D DDA-MPM-Based Fluid–Structure Interaction Method and Its Application to Hydraulic Impact on Dam Structures
Quantifying landslide risk in a low-risk region
papers.summary: The increasing availability of high-resolution, spatially distributed datasets has opened new avenues for landslide quantitative risk assessment (QRA). However, earlier large-scale studies often relied on limited input data such as temporal and magnitude landslide probability gaps, resulting in outputs of limited practical use for stakeholders. This contrasts with the growing demand for actionable, localised risk information to support landslide research and decision-making by regional policymakers. In this paper, we present a comprehensive hazard and risk assessment of soil landslides using slope-unit-based landscape partitioning. The workflow is applied to a region in Czechia, leveraging accessible national-scale datasets. Using generalised additive modelling, spatial and area probabilities of landslide occurrence are estimated, and risk maps are produced for a defined return period. In the study area, high-risk hotspots of future landslide disasters are identified. Specifically, we identified 629 buildings, with a combined estimated value of over €300 million, located within high-risk slope units. The quantified spatial probability estimates show high accuracy and low uncertainty, with a mean and standard deviation of AUC of 0.812 and 0.1, respectively, whereas the temporal probability component derived from dendrochronological analysis remains the least certain. The integration of two landslide-area scenarios with exposure and vulnerability data points out the sensitivity of risk estimates to landslide magnitude. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of QRA in regions typically considered low-risk, provided suitable datasets are available, and offers a replicable approach to inform effective risk mitigation strategies in similar environments.

papers.title: Future Management Strategies for Recurring Floods in the Global South
papers.summary: Climate-induced flooding is increasing globally as a consequence of land-use change, deforestation, floodplain encroachment, wetland reclamation, and rising greenhouse gas emissions associated with rapid urbanization and economic growth. The catastrophic 2018 floods in Kerala, India, which affected all 14 districts, resulted in widespread loss of life, infrastructure, and environmental integrity along the southwestern coast, while subsequent flooding in 2019, though less severe, continued to cause significant damage through landslides and landscape destabilization. The 2018 event triggered profound hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological alterations in the Vembanad wetland, driven by extreme monsoonal rainfall, enhanced river discharge, and a severely reduced flood-buffering capacity caused by long-term siltation and encroachment. Flooding increased water depth, turbidity, and freshwater dominance, induced hypoxic to anoxic conditions, diluted nutrients, enriched silicates, and facilitated flushing of trace metals, followed by delayed post-flood biogeochemical recovery. These changes temporarily suppressed ecosystem functioning, reduced primary productivity, promoted opportunistic and invasive species, and substantially increased https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> CO 2 , https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> CH 4 , and https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> N 2 O emissions, thereby strengthening climate feedbacks. The findings demonstrate how extreme flood events can rapidly reconfigure tropical wetland processes and compromise critical ecosystem services. The severity of impacts reflects deficiencies in watershed and water-resource management, loss of natural floodplains and vegetation, and infrastructural constraints, including compromised spillways, barrage-induced flow restriction, and obstructed drainage networks. Addressing future flood risks requires an integrated management framework combining hydrody

papers.title: Input Files for Landslide-HySEA simulations
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Input files for tsunami simulations shown in Extended Data Figure 8 with the free Tsunami-HySEA and Landslide-HySEA numerical models (https://edanya.uma.es/hysea/). The simulations shown in the paper are entirely reproducible with the input files provided here.

papers.title: Simulating Ground Vibrations Induced by Hypothetical Large Scale Slope Collapse Using Unified Geomechanical and Seismic Methods
papers.summary: This work introduces a fully deterministic, integrated multi-method framework designed to model a site-specific seismic wave propagation originating from a hypothetical future massive non-tectonic slope failure. Aimed to simulate the ground vibrations generated by a potential, abrupt ten-million-ton collapse within an open-pit mine, the framework characterizes the seismic source by coupling ground based interferometric radar monitoring with macroscopic deformation data. These datasets inform a three-dimensional stress-strain failure analysis to define representative seismic source surfaces, which subsequently drive 3D numerical modeling via the Material Point Method (MPM) to calculate the dynamic contact forces resulting from mass displacement. Next, the Spectral Element Method (SEM) is deployed to simulate mechanical wave propagation through a real geologic medium, accounting for all geometric and elastic wave effects except for intrinsic attenuation. This interconnected computational pipeline bridges large deformation geomechanics with high fidelity wave propagation; unlike existing literature that predominantly focuses on earthquake induced landslides via a SEM to MPM approach, this research introduces a novel inverse pathway (MPM to SEM) where the mining induced failure acts as the primary seismic source. By embedding complex 3D topographies, multi-layered geological interfaces, and heterogeneous lithological variations directly into the elastic model, the framework accurately captures site-specific phenomena, such as surface wave amplification, geometric spreading, and structural attenuation, up to a high frequency limit of 15 Hz. Ultimately, the model successfully quantifies localized ground motion variations in terms of peak velocity, peak acceleration, and complex waveforms across the domain, offering a robust tool for future risk assessment in nearby critical infrastructure.

papers.title: LANDSLIDE SUSCEPTIBILITY MAPPING AND PREDICTION UNCERTAINTY USING EXPLAINABLE DEEP LEARNING BASED ON SENTINEL-1 AND TOPOGRAPHIC DERIVATIVES IN SOUTHEAST SULAWESI
papers.source: Simtek jurnal sistem informasi dan teknik komputer
papers.summary: Landslide assessment in Southeast Sulawesi requires susceptibility information that not only indicates risk classes but also explains the prediction basis and model confidence levels. This study employs an "Expectable Deep Learning" development workflow by integrating Sentinel-1 GRD data and topographic derivatives. The initial inventory comprises 54 points across three susceptibility classes; 34 points fall within the raster coverage, forming 128×128 pixel patches with nine channels: VV, VH, RVI, NDPI, CR, elevation, slope, aspect, and curvature. A Light CNN serves as the baseline, while a Squeeze-and-Excitation CNN is used to test attention enhancement. Model interpretability is addressed using Grad-CAM and SHAP (based on a Random Forest surrogate), while uncertainty is quantified via Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensemble methods. The Light CNN achieved 50.00% accuracy, 61.11% macro-precision, 50.00% macro-recall, 52.22% macro-F1, and an AUC-ROC of 45.83%. Although the model achieved 96.38% training accuracy, validation loss rose to 2.0872, indicating overfitting. Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensemble yielded average normalized entropy values ​​of 0.9634 and 0.9976, respectively. Inference across 500 grid positions resulted in 28 low, 31 medium, and 441 high susceptibility classifications; however, 42% of positions exhibited normalized entropy of at least 0.90. The results demonstrate the successful integration of classification, interpretability, and uncertainty assessment; however, the resulting map remains experimental and requires refinement through expanded raster coverage, the addition of verified inventory data, and spatial validation.

papers.title: Type-Resolved Landslide Modeling with PS-InSAR Deformation and Multi-Decadal Optical Surface Change
papers.summary: Large earthquakes leave mountain cities exposed to rockfalls, debris flows, and slides that can remain active or reactivate for decades. However, susceptibility assessments often pool these processes, use validation designs that ignore spatial dependence, and are seldom compared with satellite observations. This study presents a type-resolved multi-sensor landslide assessment for Muzaffarabad, a Himalayan city severely affected by the 2005 Mw 7.6 Kashmir earthquake. Using 274 landslides from the area and 16 conditioning factors, type-specific and pooled models were built with random forest (RF) and a sparse fuzzy additive model (SFAM) and evaluated with spatial block cross-validation that grouped linked landslides, prevalence-aware metrics and corrected significance tests. Type-specific RF models reached spatial areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.77–0.80 and placed 55–62% of held-out landslides in the highest-ranked 20% of the area, with discrimination similar to that of pooled models; the rockfall and debris flow models were more type-specific, capturing 8–21 percentage points fewer landslides of other types under random validation, with less certain differences under spatial validation. SFAM provided interpretable factor-response curves and discrimination comparable to RF for rockfalls and debris flows. At the slope-unit scale, cluster exclusion and buffering reduced RF AUC by 0.06–0.15. Sentinel-1 PS-InSAR (2014–2021) detected motion within 50 m of all four known creep sites and in 157 observable slope units; across the observable terrain, however, motion was not more frequent in high-susceptibility units (odds ratios 0.70–0.81, p ≥ 0.12). Landsat and Sentinel-2 records traced scar persistence and revegetation and identified 16 new or renewed disturbances, all confirmed on dated imagery; at Domeshi, slow deformation detected by radar preceded the 2023 failure. Susceptibility maps rank landslide-affected terrain, PS-InSAR identifies

papers.title: Slope Classes by District and Block, Meghalaya
papers.summary: Map dividing Meghalaya into 238,778 areas by slope class, each with its description, district, block and area. Published on the Meghalaya State GeoHub. The period it covers is not stated. Detail is by small mapped area within each block. It is useful for judging how steep land is, for example when planning roads, farming or landslide risk. Downloads freely from the Meghalaya State GeoHub's public map service, with no sign-in.

papers.title: The giant landslide in Niscemi (Italy): history and geomatics reveal its 17th- century anthropogenic roots
papers.summary: The recent reactivation of the Niscemi (Sicily) giant deep-seated landslide in January 2026, following a similar event in 1997, highlights a complex geomorphological setting with an evolution dating back centuries. Historical sources document a massive 1790 event that severely damaged the town's outskirts. However, due to a recognized structural gap in bridging pre-industrial historical evidence with modern spatial analysis, the exact spatial extent and the long-term anthropogenic preconditioning of this 18th-century failure remained largely unexplored. By combining critical analysis of historical archives with modern geomatics, we achieve two primary outcomes. First, we backdate the initial slope instability to a critical precursor event in 1776 and accurately geolocate the spatial extension of the subsequent 1790 landslide crown. Second, through detailed analysis of multi-century cadastral records (1600–1800), we correlate a marked demographic increase with radical deforestation and hydrographic modifications, suggesting that pre-industrial land-use changes critically preconditioned the hydrogeological hazard. In doing so, we also refute a two-century-old historiographical error that erroneously attributed the 1790 collapse to a tectonic earthquake. Ultimately, this study provides a generalizable methodology to spatially resolve the anthropogenic impact on deep-seated landslides, yielding crucial baselines to design geomorphologically and ecologically sound mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Automatic classification of landslide seismic signals based on multimodal time–frequency analysis and deep residual shrinkage networks
Landslide Susceptibility Assessment Using Frequency Ratio (FR) Model in the Upper Koyna River Basin, Western Maharashtra, India
papers.summary: Landslides represent a significant geo-environmental hazard in mountainous and tectonically active regions, posing threats to human life, infrastructure, and ecosystems. This study assesses landslide susceptibility in the upper Koyna River basin, Maharashtra, using the Frequency Ratio (FR) model, a bivariate statistical method that correlates historical landslide occurrences with various causative factors. The study area, extending from the Koyna River's source in Mahabaleshwar to Patan town, is characterized by rugged ridge topography, steep gradients, and substantial rainfall, making it inherently vulnerable to slope failures. Anthropogenic influences, including dam construction, deforestation, mining, and road development, have further aggravated the instability of the landscape. The FR model was applied to integrate and analyze multiple thematic layers such as slope, lithology, soil type, land use/land cover (LULC), lineament density, rainfall distribution, and proximity to rivers and roads. The model calculates the ratio of landslide occurrence within each class of these factors relative to their spatial distribution across the study area, allowing for the identification of zones with varying degrees of susceptibility. Results classified the region into four susceptibility zones: low, moderate, high, and very high. The central and southern parts of the basin exhibited the highest vulnerability, mainly due to steep gradients, weak geological formations, poor drainage conditions, and intense human intervention. Validation of the susceptibility map using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve yielded an Area Under the Curve (AUC) value of 0.788, indicating strong predictive accuracy of the model. The generated landslide susceptibility map is a vital tool for local authorities, planners, and policymakers for risk assessment, disaster mitigation, and sustainable land use planning. The findings emphasize the need for regulated development and targeted cons

papers.title: Structural controls of two townships in the Otway Ranges and the use of domains to inform residential landslide risk assessment
papers.summary: On Christmas Day, 2015, a bushfire significantly impacted the townships of Wye River and Separation Creek in the Otway Ranges. Over 100 houses were destroyed across the two townships, and not all properties were redeveloped. The towns are located within the Colac Otway Shire (COS), which has a long-established Erosion Management Overlay (EMO) which is effectively a landslide hazard overlay. This overlay requires that development be “undertaken at a tolerable risk to human life and property from landslip” in accordance with the Australian Geomechanics Society Practice Note Guidelines for Landslide Risk Management 2007. Post-fire conditions improved slope access allowing for township-scale structural mapping. The townships are underlain by the Cretaceous Eumeralla Formation, a folded sequence of interbedded sedimentary rocks. Slope formation processes and landslides in this bedrock are generally controlled by bedding dip and direction, and the interaction with shear and fault zones. While conducting over 20 Landslide Risk Assessments (LRAs) in the township the author progressively established and refined the structural domains within the area to effectively characterise landslide hazards. These domains may improve the efficiency of landslide characterisation and reduce potential data and landslide hazard biases for future developments.

papers.title: National-scale debris-flow hazard indication modelling for Swiss railway infrastructure
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Debris flows are among the most destructive alpine hazards, threatening settlements and critical infrastructure with average annual damages in Switzerland of CHF 321 million. Hazard indication modelling of debris flows, among other hazards, offers the possibility to identify hazard hot spots at a regional and national scale. Additionally it lays the foundation for future scenario modelling. We present the Large-Scale Hazard Indication Modelling (LSHIM) framework for debris flows as commissioned by the Swiss federal railway (SBB) with guiding value return periods of 30, 100, and 300 years. For susceptibility modelling, we combine high-resolution digital terrain models, climatic and geologic layers, and statistical modelling with a random forest approach. Susceptibility is cross-validated against the Swiss event database (StorMe) with an average accuracy of 81.4 % and application results in 16 756 possible release areas. Dynamic runout is calculated with a tailored version of RAMMS::Debrisflow, where we define hydrograph volume from MeteoSchweiz-modelled extreme precipitation. Landscape erosivity is assessed by geology and geomorphology. Results indicate 55, 76, and 85 km of railway affected by debris flow hazard for a 30-, 100-, and 300-year return period, respectively. The highest intensity class shows the highest relative increase under longer return periods. This approach enables a large-scale hazard indication assessment based on high-quality input data. The results are a valuable base for further planning and investigations that incorporate climate change. Limitations in the methodology lie in the static definition of release area and deterministic parameterization.

papers.title: Remote sensing as a tool for assessing landslide impacts on coastal waters at Porchat Island (SE Brazil)
papers.summary: On April 29, 2025, a water pipeline rupture on Porchat Island (São Vicente, southeastern Brazil) triggered a mass movement that released sediment into adjacent coastal waters. Effects of urban infrastructure failures on coastal water quality are rarely documented with imagery of adequate spatial and temporal resolution. We used Sentinel-2 and PlanetScope, processed in ACOLITE, to estimate turbidity, suspended matter concentration (SMC), chlorophyll-a, and Secchi disk depth before and after the rupture, relating the sediment plume to meteoceanographic conditions. In Sentinel-2 images, median SMC in the waters adjacent to the island increased from 9.0 to 19.0 g/m³ and median Secchi depth decreased from 2.07 to 1.03 m, whereas changes in Santos and São Vicente bays were smaller. In PlanetScope images, SMC increased the day after the rupture, most markedly near the island and in Santos Bay, and by May 2 had fallen below the pre-event levels of April 27, which were already elevated after the late-April rainfall. Chlorophyll-a varied among dates without a clear response. As no in situ data were available, results are interpreted as relative changes. PlanetScope’s daily revisit showed the sediment plume shrinking from 7.50 km² on April 30 to 2.02 km² on May 2 and dispersing toward central Santos Bay under waves from the southeast and south quadrants. This case shows that an infrastructure failure can cause marked but apparently temporary changes in the optical properties of coastal waters, and indicates that high-frequency, high-resolution remote sensing is useful for rapid impact assessment and for supporting coastal monitoring.

papers.title: Piles of Sand, Piles of Beads, and Piles of…
Mind the Gap: Overview of Key Findings of the 2026 Media Capture Monitoring Reports Measuring EMFA Compliance
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: The 2026 Media Capture Monitoring Reports reveal a highly uneven picture across the eight countries covered by this overview. More than a year after the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA) became fully applicable, Finland is the only country in the sample where the national framework needed to apply the EMFA’s core provisions is fully in place and functioning. Following the change in government, Hungary adopted substantial amendments in June 2026 addressing public service media governance and regulatory independence, but their practical effectiveness remains untested and important gaps remain on state funding and media pluralism. Greece enacted two laws strengthening the transparency of both media ownership and state advertising, but implementation is incomplete while concerns persist regarding the independence of the media regulator and public service media. In Poland, Spain and Bulgaria, reform has advanced mainly on paper: governments have prepared draft legislation or announced reforms, but the relevant measures have not yet entered into force. Romania made no progress towards national implementation. Finally, Slovakia presents a different and more troubling pattern: although national rules and institutions exist, the year was marked by a deterioration in the practical independence of both public service media and the regulator, making the country the EU Member State in the sample that has been experiencing the most rapidly deteriorating media capture climate. This uneven implementation means that the effectiveness of the EMFA itself still cannot be assessed consistently across the sample states. In most countries, the principal findings concern the absence, delay or incompleteness of national measures rather than the performance of a fully operational EMFA framework. Moreover, some of the most significant changes in 2026 were the result of domestic political developments rather than of the Regulation. This is particularly evident in Hungary, where a landslide ele

papers.source: Bulletin of Engineering Geology and the Environment

papers.title: Current Developments and Challenges in the State of AI and Machine Learning-Based Landslide Susceptibility Prediction Models: An Overview
papers.summary: This review article covers all current developments within the disciplines of AI and ML as they relate to the generation of landslide susceptibility maps. The AI and ML methodologies discussed will feature many of the most widely used techniques today, such as random forests (RF), support vector machines (SVM), gradient boosting machines (GBM), as well as artificial neural networks (ANN), but will also include many recent advances related to hybrid and ensemble learning techniques. The area within this review where methodological advancement is most needed is data preparation, feature engineering, and model validation and testing; the interaction between GIS and AI/ML models will provide additional insights into these challenges for future methodologies. The greatest contribution this review can provide to the field of landslide susceptibility modeling is a comparison between traditional AI and ML methods and the newer deep learning techniques and the increasingly popular interpretable AI-based models outlined in this review; further analysis will clarify the advantages and weaknesses of both approaches.

papers.title: Experimental insight into scale effects in 3D granular slides
papers.summary: Granular slides, including landslides, snow avalanches and rockfalls, are often investigated in the controlled laboratory environment. However, limited knowledge is currently available about scale effects, typically resulting in major deviations between the upscaled laboratory and nature observations. This study quantifies scale effects in unconfined (3D) dry granular slides of up to 54.25 kg, using a 3 m long ramp transitioning into a horizontal runout area. Four Froude scale series, S1–S4, were conducted involving experiments at scales 1:1 (reference), 1:2 and 1:4, on either smooth (S1, S2) or rough surfaces (S3, S4). The slide kinematics and deposit​ characteristics were determined with video analysis, photogrammetry and direct measurement techniques. Significant scale effects for the slide velocities and runout distances R s of up to 45% and 27%, respectively, have been identified. However, scale effects are significantl​y less dominant for S3 and S4, likely related to the slide regime transition from liquid to gaseous. R s collapse in dimensionless form together with previous laboratory and nature data on a master curve proposed by Kesseler et al. (2020) for 2D, when normalised with the grain Reynolds number. Involving the bed friction angle in the normalisation did not result in significant further improvements confirming that scale effects are mainly related to the Reynolds number. Finally, an example b​ased on the 2007 Mount Steele slide illustrates how the master curve can be applied to predict R s at nature, and other scales, useful for landslide hazard assessment.

papers.title: Supplementary material to "Coupling modeled colluvium depth, landslide initiation, and debris-flow runout to map regional-scale inundation susceptibility"
Joint data-mechanism failure probability assessment and reinforcement strategy for distribution networks under multi-hazard coupling
Source Dynamics of the 2017 Greenland Landslide From Force‐Time Inversion With Ambient‐Noise‐Constrained Velocity Models
papers.source: Journal of Geophysical Research Earth Surface
papers.summary: The 2017 Nuugaatsiaq landslide in Greenland represents a critical case for investigating the source dynamics and associated hazards of large Arctic landslides. This landslide generated strong broadband seismic waves as well as monochromatic signals associated with a seiche, a standing‐wave oscillation of water in the fjord. Here, we use ambient seismic noise cross‐correlations to measure surface wave dispersion and construct path‐specific one‐dimensional velocity models. Theoretical Green's functions calculated from these models are then used in a frequency‐domain inversion of the landslide force‐time function. A controlled comparison yields variance reductions of 51.10%, 68.52%, and 74.49% for IASP91, CRUST1.0, and the ambient seismic noise‐constrained models, respectively. The improvement over IASP91 is clear, whereas the additional improvement over CRUST1.0 is modest and varies among paths and components: 14 of 21 traces improve, including the east component on all seven paths and all three components at UPNV and SUMG. The recovered force history lasts approximately 100 s and contains an early vertical‐force pulse, a stronger positive excursion at approximately 25–40 s, and subsequent polarity reversals. These results provide new seismological constraints on the source dynamics of the 2017 Nuugaatsiaq landslide and demonstrate the potential value of independently constrained path‐specific velocity models for force‐time inversion in data‐sparse or structurally complex regions.

papers.title: Causal Subspace Detection and Reconstruction with Protected Local Deformation Modes in GNSS Time Series
papers.summary: Preserving weak deformation while detecting observation faults remains challenging in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) monitoring. We develop Joint, a causal subspace framework combining protected local offsets and linear rates, dual-timescale background learning, covariance whitening, historical contamination control, matched-subspace detection, and masked generalized least-squares reconstruction. Only observations available at the decision epoch are used, and missing observations are selected before whitening. Theoretical analysis establishes residual invariance and preservation of protected components under fixed-model, fixed-support, and full-rank reconstruction conditions. Evaluation uses three synthetic scenarios with 20 random seeds each and nine receivers at six sites. Historical contamination control increases F1 by 0.093–0.190 and reduces reconstruction root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 0.232–0.307 mm relative to its removal. Joint achieves event recall of 92.81–98.13%, exceeding HampelAxis with more false positives. Field injections transmit a 1 mm plateau as 0.999855–1.000000 mm, although maximum transition RMSE reaches 1.8276 mm. These results support explicit protection of prescribed motion components and suppression of historical contamination, while identifying calibration and transient response as limitations. Joint provides an interpretable workflow for GNSS quality control and displacement tracking, with potential applications in landslide, mining-subsidence, and structural monitoring.

papers.title: Coupling Local Moran’s I with multi-relational graph convolutional networks for landslide susceptibility evaluation by a spatial autocorrelation guided paradigm
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility evaluation (LSE) is crucial for preventing geological risks, yet existing methods fall short in modeling the phenomenon of spatial autocorrelation. This work proposes a Local Moran’s I guided multi-relational graph convolutional network (Moran-RGCN) method, which integrates spatial statistical theory with artificial intelligence technique. In constructing graph nodes, slope units are represented as nodes in a graph structure; the Local Moran’s I is employed to optimize the initial adjacency graph and construct a multi-relational graph structure. Finally, a relational graph convolutional network (RGCN) captures these relational dependencies, enabling more explicit modeling of spatial autocorrelation and producing accurate and reliable LSE results. We evaluated this method using the landslide inventory of Ya’an City, Sichuan Province, China. The Moran-RGCN model outperforms existing methods such as Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and location-driven Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The model demonstrated superior performance, achieving an accuracy of ( 90.89 ± 0.71 ) % and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of ( 94.79 ± 0.30 ) % , while the generated susceptibility maps exhibited more concentrated hotspots. The mapped predictions assigned larger proportions of slope units to both the lower and higher susceptibility classes than the compared models, while the lower susceptibility areas contained fewer known landslide occurrences and the higher susceptibility areas captured more known landslide occurrences. Our research demonstrates that the Moran-RGCN mode incorporating Local Moran’ s I effectively reduces redundant connections and noise propagation. This achieves a refined representation of spatial autocorrelation, enhancing the accuracy, reliability, and interpretability of LSE.

papers.title: Investigating the landslide-inducing precipitation conditions in China: spatio-temporal analysis and multiple thresholds modeling
papers.summary: Landslides are widespread natural hazards and have become a focus of global attention. In China, due to mountainous terrain and monsoon climate, nearly 70% of fatal landslide events are caused by precipitation. Studies on the characteristics of precipitation that induce landslides are of significance for risk prevention and mitigation. However, such studies are relatively scarce. This paper, based on 1,239 historical landslide records from 1991 to 2024, and utilizing a high-resolution rainfall dataset — MSWEP — extracted landslide-inducing precipitation events (PreLS) and conducted a comprehensive analysis of their spatiotemporal characteristics. Precipitation-induced landslides in China are primarily concentrated in the Sichuan Basin, the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, the Middle-Lower Yangtze Plain, and the Loess Plateau, with the highest frequency occurring during the summer. PreLS lasting more than three days are associated with over 73% of the documented landslide events in China. In recent years, with the intensification of precipitation extremes, both the cumulative precipitation before landslides and the triggering precipitation on the event day, as well as antecedent precipitation, have increased significantly across most regions. Based on regional hydro-climatic and geomorphological characteristics, we establish regionally differentiated event-duration (E-D) and triggering-antecedent precipitation (Pt-AP) thresholds. Independent temporal validation demonstrates their high recall capability for documented landslides, providing a quantitative reference for regionally targeted landslide hazard monitoring and preliminary early warning.

papers.title: Data and code for: Fold structure, bedding and landslides in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bangladesh
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Data and analysis code supporting the article "Fold structure, bedding and landslides in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bangladesh" (Zaman and Raveed, submitted to Natural Hazards). The package contains 52 anticline axes digitised from Wang et al. (2014), bedding attitudes digitised from Hossain et al. (2024), derived structural layers (limb position, bedding dip direction, distance to anticline axes; 30 m, UTM 46N), the Python and Google Earth Engine scripts used for all analyses, the results of every statistical test reported in the article, and the article figures. Online Resource 1 (supplementary information) is included as a PDF. Third-party data (the landslide inventory of Rabby and Li 2020, the USGS geological map, Copernicus DEM, Sentinel-2, CHIRPS, ESA WorldCover and OpenStreetMap) are not redistributed; sources are listed in README.txt.

papers.title: Terrain-modulated saturation-driven mobility amplification of rainfall-induced shallow landslides
Runout Dynamics Simulation of a Loess Landslide Combining Limit Equilibrium and Dynamic Numerical Methods
papers.summary: Tension cracks and sinkholes near a proposed transmission tower site on the Gaojiamao loess slope in Shaanxi Province, China, raise concerns about slope stability and potential failure consequences. Engineering geological investigations and unmanned aerial vehicle surveys were integrated with GeoStudio stability analysis and Massflow runout simulation. The initial sliding mass was constrained by the potential slip surface, surface cracks, and topographic boundaries. The circular slip surface search gives factors of safety of 1.53 and 1.13 under natural and rainfall conditions, respectively. The noncircular search gives factors of safety of 1.57 and 1.17, respectively. The circular surface gives the lowest values among the mechanisms examined, with the rainfall result indicating an inadequate engineering safety reserve. Under the specified initial geometry and dynamic parameters, simulated motion comprised initiation and acceleration, deceleration and deposition, and subsequent localized adjustment. The peak volume-weighted mean velocity was 1.66 m/s, the spatial maximum velocity was 21.83 m/s, and localized motion remained at 45 s. The maximum horizontal runout distance was approximately 104.7 m. Most material accumulated on the lower loess terrace, while some frontal material entered the river channel. An approximately 5 m local thickness reduction indicates a severe potential loss of shallow-foundation support at the proposed tower site. Within the ±20% parameter combination range, the friction coefficient had a pronounced influence on runout distance and cumulative river entry volume. These scenario results identify potential impacts on the tower site and river channel.

papers.title: Radar observations reveals recurrent and evolving transient responses of slow-moving landslides to successive moderate seismicity
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: The comprehensive dataset was compiled to support research on exploring the recurrent transient responses of slow-moving landslides to clustered moderate seismicity. It contains the comprehensive InSAR multi-track products and landslide inventory used to investigate the dynamic evolutionary trajectories of 332 slow-moving landslides in the Colca River Valley, southeastern Peru (2016–2024).Data structure:1. Slow-moving landslide Inventory (Vector Data)landslide_332/: A subfolder containing the Shapefile (.shp and its auxiliary files) delineating the boundaries and spatial distribution of the 332 identified slow-moving landslides within the study area.2. InSAR Deformation Velocity Maps (Raster Data in GeoTIFF format)Vlos_T25.tif: Line-of-sight (LOS) annual deformation velocity derived from Sentinel-1 ascending Track 25.Vlos_T47.tif: Line-of-sight (LOS) annual deformation velocity derived from Sentinel-1 descending Track 47.Vlos_T127.tif: Line-of-sight (LOS) annual deformation velocity derived from Sentinel-1 descending Track 127.Vslope.tif: Down-slope projected annual deformation velocity map, transformed from the multi-track InSAR observations.3. seismic.txt: Metadata of regional seismic events (M≥4.0) utilized to define the seismic moment release index.

papers.title: Multi-Temporal Monitoring of an Active Landslide Affecting Waste-Management Infrastructure Using Total-Station Geodesy and UAV-LiDAR at the CMID Dobrin Site, Romania
papers.summary: Landslides that develop inside or next to waste-management facilities affect not only the ground but also the infrastructure built on it, yet quantitative multi-temporal monitoring of such sites is rarely reported. We re-analyzed a four-epoch dataset (December 2025 to August 2026) from the CMID Dobrin integrated waste-management center, Sălaj County, Romania, consisting of a 66-point robotic total-station network and UAV-LiDAR surveys, with a UAV orthophoto used for network design. Horizontal and three-dimensional displacements, equivalent velocities and azimuths were computed from the coordinates for every point and interval. Because the intervals differ in length (about 2, 2 and 4 months), movement rates rather than raw displacements were compared. The network median velocity did not increase (3.6, 4.1 and 2.9 mm/month), but a small cluster of points moved much faster in April–August 2026, reaching 43.7 mm/month at R53 and 28.0 mm/month at R47; the cumulative horizontal displacement at R53 was 175.7 mm. The largest subsidence (−58 mm at R40 by April 2026, −41 mm by August) occurred in a partly offset zone. An indicative detection threshold of 5.2–6.9 mm, derived from the Rayleigh distribution of the horizontal displacement magnitude, and a reference-frame check that revealed common epoch-to-epoch offsets, mainly in height, show that network-wide signals of a few millimeters should be read with caution. The LiDAR products agree with the geodetic pattern at the level of surface morphology, but a DEM of difference, computed after correcting a vertical-datum inconsistency between the models, could not resolve the measured vertical movements (level of detection about ±0.18 m). The geodetic data describe the surface kinematics of the movement; its geotechnical context, a slow, deep-seated slide on a slip surface at about 7 m depth in active silty clays, is taken from an independent geotechnical expertise of the site.

papers.title: Spatial validation and geological coverage effects in machine learning-based landslide hazard map reproduction in Central Papua
papers.source: International Journal of Engineering Science and Information Technology
papers.summary: Machine learning is increasingly used for landslide susceptibility mapping, yet evaluation by random data splitting can overstate performance when samples are spatially autocorrelated and some predictors cover the study area only partially. This study applies an integrated evaluation framework that separates the effect of spatial data splitting from that of hyperparameter tuning and diagnoses the role of incomplete geological coverage. The framework was used to reproduce the national inaRISK landslide hazard zoning in Nabire, Paniai, and Mimika Regencies, Central Papua, Indonesia. A balanced sample of 1,500 points in three hazard classes was linked to six environmental factors, including slope, elevation, rainfall, land cover, and lithology. Logistic regression, support vector machine, and random forest models were compared under random, spatial, and nested spatial cross-validation, supplemented by block-count sensitivity, geology ablation, and class-specific and ordinal metrics. Under random validation, random forest reached 73.7% accuracy. Under nested spatial validation, accuracy fell to 63.6–65.9% for all three models, and block-bootstrap intervals for accuracy differences included zero, so no model could be shown to be superior. With outer splits kept identical within each scheme, the random–spatial gap was 6.9–8.9 points, far larger than the global–nested tuning gap of 0.3–1.2 points. The moderate class was the hardest to recognise, and severe confusions between the low and high classes stayed at 9.0–10.1%. Of the 500 high-class points, 369 lay outside geological coverage; coverage status itself carried predictive information, and the contribution of geology shrank on spatial test data. In practice, a partially mapped predictor can act as a location marker, so its coverage should be reported before its contribution is interpreted. Studies that train models on reference maps should report nested spatial validation, and the present findings concern reference-map

papers.title: EMA-YOLO: attention-guided feature fusion and space-to-depth downsampling for landslide detection
papers.summary: Landslides and exposed terrain with similar optical appearances complicate automated landslide inventory mapping. We developed EMA-YOLO from YOLOv8s by adding efficient multi-scale attention to the neck, replacing selected backbone downsampling layers with space-to-depth convolution, and adopting Wise-IoU v3 for box regression. Experiments used 1393 landslide images and 3,003 negative images from Gongliu and Bijie, with source groups separated before training augmentation. On the held-out test set, EMA-YOLO achieved 93.01% AP 50, 93.82% precision, 92.29% recall, and 93.05% F1. YOLOv8s recorded 90.03% AP 50 on the same test set. Relative to YOLOv8s, small-object AP 50 increased from 55.39% to 61.82%, and the fraction of negative test images with false detections decreased from 6.00% to 3.33%. In a separate YOLOv8s experiment, training-image composition increased the number of images in which every annotated landslide was detected from 73 to 92 out of 104 held-out natural multiple-landslide images. On the Luding test set, EMA-YOLO achieved 81.0% AP 50 with direct transfer, 90.4% after fine-tuning with 69 Luding images, and 91.0% with 161 images. These results support candidate landslide screening in the evaluated imagery.

papers.summary: [FR] La tradition chinoise raconte que Gun tenta en vain de contenir un grand déluge par des digues, avant que son fils Yu le maîtrise en creusant des canaux. Wu et coll. J.-C. un glissement de terrain barrant le fleuve Jaune, dont la rupture aurait provoqué une crue exceptionnelle, et relient cet événement à la tradition. L'existence historique de la dynastie Xia n'est pas traitée. Préprint non évalué par les pairs — résultats indicatifs. [EN] Chinese tradition tells that Gun tried in vain to contain a great flood with dykes before his son Yu mastered it by digging channels. Wu et al. (2016) propose that an earthquake triggered around 1920 BC a landslide damming the Yellow River, whose failure would have caused an exceptional flood, and link this event to the tradition. This critical narrative review compares five readings; the 'repeated floods' reading scores highest (10/12), ahead of the outburst flood (9/12). The historical existence of the Xia dynasty is not treated. Preprint not peer-reviewed — indicative results.
