papers.title: Development of Rainfall–R-factor Models and Trend Analysis of Rainfall Erosivity across Selected Agro-Ecological Sub-Regions of India
papers.summary: Reduced agricultural yields and nutrient depletion are consequences of soil erosion, which is worsened by climate change. This calls for precise soil erosion measurement, in an agrarian country like India. The rainfall erosivity factor (R-factor) is an important component of the widely used universal soil loss equation (USLE) for quantifying potential soil. In comparision to the Modified Fournier Index (MFI) or hourly and daily rainfall data, the R-factor calculated based I 30 derived from sub-hourly rainfall data is more accurate. However, still, most locations do not have sub-hourly rainfall information available. Therefore, in this study, rainfall-R-factor models were developed for eight Agro-Ecological Sub Regions (AESRs) of India (3.0, 4.1, 4.4, 5.2, 9.1, 12.1, 14.2 and 19.2). Further, for analyzing temporal trends in erosive rainfall and R-factor, Innovative Trend Analysis (ITA) and Mann-Kendall (MK) were used. While the other AESRs showed a power relationship, AESRs 4.4 and 9.1 showed a linear relationship between annual rainfall and annual R-factor. Six AESRs (3.0, 4.1, 4.4, 5.2, 12.1 and 14.2) exhibited increasing trends for both erosive rainfall and R-factor, while AESRs 9.1 and 19.2 exhibited decreasing trends. R-factors calculated from IMDAA hourly rainfall data were generally lower than the I 30 based R-factor, except for the low rainfall regions. The monthly erosivity density during monsoon exceeded the critical threshold in all AESRs indicating a substantial risk of water-induced soil erosion. The findings confirm the necessity for localised rainfall-R-factor models and soil and water conservation strategies.

papers.title: Coupling modeled colluvium depth, landslide initiation, and debris-flow runout to map regional-scale inundation susceptibility
papers.summary: In post-glacial mountain landscapes, shallow landslides can transition into debris flows that threaten communities and infrastructure. Landslide susceptibility maps are important for identifying where landslides may occur and mitigating landslide risk, but regional-scale models often rely on first-order terrain metrics, such as slope and relief, and may not resolve local topographic controls on landslide initiation. Furthermore, landslide susceptibility models are rarely coupled with runout models to identify potential downslope inundation. Here, we coupled a physics-based landslide initiation model with a regional-scale runout model to estimate potential debris flow inundation across a large swath of Prince of Wales Island, Alaska. Using a high-resolution digital terrain model, the initiation model estimated groundwater conditions from topographic wetness and simulated spatially variable colluvium depth using models for soil production and transport. Compared with a landslide inventory, the initiation model exhibited strong discriminatory skill between inventoried initiation points and non-landslide terrain (AUC = 0.86), highlighting how spatially variable colluvium and groundwater conditions can distinguish potentially unstable convergent terrain from surrounding steep terrain. We calibrated debris-flow entrainment parameters independently within HUC-14 watersheds by optimizing agreement between modeled and inventoried landslides, capturing spatial variability in debris-flow mobility across the study area. Our results also indicate that modeled colluvium depth can be used to inform sediment availability for debris-flow entrainment, extending the utility of modeled colluvium beyond landslide initiation. The resulting debris-flow susceptibility maps estimate potential inundation at spatial scales relevant to assessing the exposure of roads, infrastructure, and communities to landslide hazards. These maps were developed through iterative collaboration with Tribal gov

papers.title: Beyond Incidental Response: Strengthening Disaster Preparedness In Talang Paruh Merangin Jambi UNESCO Global Geopark
papers.summary: Talang Paruh Village in Lembah Masurai Sub-district lies within the Merangin Jambi UNESCO Global Geopark and is exposed to flooding, landslides, and seismic hazards. This community service programme aimed to identify locally perceived preparedness gaps, strengthen practical preparedness capacity, and initiate an institutional pathway for sustained village-level disaster preparedness. A participatory approach was implemented from 17 to 19 July 2026 through community engagement, participatory discussion, preparedness outreach with the Indonesian Red Cross, and a technical session with the Merangin Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency. Approximately 40 participants represented the village government, customary and community leaders, youth, women’s groups, and local organisations. The programme identified three major gaps: no established evacuation routes, no standard operating procedure for disaster preparedness and emergency response, and an underdeveloped village preparedness structure. Participants also prioritised simulation and technical training. The programme did not establish a completed preparedness system; rather, it generated a context-specific agenda for evacuation-route planning, emergency procedures, a village preparedness structure, regular simulation, and continued technical coordination. These findings indicate that the principal challenge is institutional capacity to translate existing awareness and willingness into sustained village preparedness.

papers.title: Influence of the Representation of Structural Discontinuities on Open-Pit Slope Stability Assessment: A Case Study of a Limestone Quarry
papers.summary: Structural discontinuities are a significant factor affecting the stability of rock slopes, governing the development of potential failure mechanisms. This study examined how alternative representations of structural discontinuities in numerical models affect back-analysis results, the resulting equivalent strength parameters, and the interpretation of predicted failure mechanisms. The analyses were conducted on the southern slope of the Miedzianka Devonian limestone open-pit mine. The study included geological and structural mapping, laboratory strength testing of landslide material, and back-analysis of a landslide that occurred in 2017. Slope stability analyses were performed using the finite element method (FEM) in a two-dimensional framework, employing the shear strength reduction (SSR) technique. Additionally, a three-dimensional stability analysis of wedge sliding was conducted using the limit equilibrium method. The back-analysis yielded factors of safety of 1.00 for the model with reduced strength parameters applied to the entire rock mass and 1.03 for the model explicitly incorporating bedding and fault planes. The results indicate that similar factors of safety can be obtained from back-analysis under different assumptions regarding the representation of structural discontinuities and the strength properties of the rock mass. The calibrated parameters were subsequently used to assess the stability of five slope cross-sections under current and final slope geometries, revealing substantial variations in the results. In cross-section 1–1′, without considering the overburden, the factor of safety decreased from 3.09 to 0.33. These findings indicate that rock slope stability assessments should not rely solely on the factor of safety but should also account for how identified structural discontinuities are represented in numerical models.

papers.title: Petrogenic carbon oxidation from the mountains to floodplains: implications for carbon balance in a large river basin
Interpretable machine learning with dual-source contrast sampling for rainfall-related slope instability susceptibility assessment in Aba Prefecture, China
papers.summary: This study addresses sampling bias and exposure-induced shortcut variables in landslide susceptibility modelling for rainfall-related slope failures. A data-driven framework integrates dual-source mechanism-contrast sample construction with two-stage susceptibility–exposure separation, evaluated on 10,644 samples (5,322 instability records and 5,322 constructed contrasts) from Aba Prefecture, southwestern China. The inventory comprises debris flows (41.4%), landslides (39.0%), and unstable slopes (19.6%), with 66.1% documenting compound earthquake–rainfall triggers. Random-forest distinguishability analysis yielded an AUC-ROC of 0.965 for the dual-source contrast set, compared with 1.000 under pure spatial sampling, the latter denoting trivially separable classes. Fault distance was calculated for both positive and contrast samples and included as a susceptibility predictor. Among seventeen models, the AUC-weighted voting ensemble attains the highest F1 (0.923), and the highest AUC-ROC of 0.973 is achieved by default LightGBM, tuned LightGBM, and tuned XGBoost. A paired random-versus-spatial cross-validation comparison (5-fold 2D KMeans blocks) shows that spatial blocking reduces AUC by only 1.2–1.6% and leaves F1 essentially unchanged, while a coordinate ablation changes AUC by at most 0.004 when longitude and latitude are removed. Group-level Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) identify terrain (59.3%), rainfall (19.1%), and vegetation (6.4%) as the dominant feature families, with coordinates contributing 5.8% and fault distance 3.3%; these are model-learned associations rather than verified causal mechanisms. Classifying out-of-fold susceptibility probabilities into five relative classes highlights the southeastern study area as the highest-scoring region. Priority weighting is restricted to records carrying documented exposure data, which are unavailable for spatially sampled locations.

papers.title: Rainfall-triggered railway earthwork instability: thresholds, hydrologic state and operational warning
papers.summary: Purpose Rainfall-triggered failures of railway embankments, cuttings and adjacent slopes are managed through rainfall thresholds, geotechnical assessment, monitoring and operating rules, but these elements are often evaluated separately. This review examines how the railway-earthwork evidence progresses from rainfall exposure through hydrologic state and physical response to operational action. Design/methodology/approach A structured critical evidence review was reconstructed from 596 screened records. Of 274 records advanced to the full-text stage, 105 verified full texts were assessed, 20 were excluded after full-text review, 169 had no verified full text and 85 studies were retained. Primary-objective coding was retained for description, while the principal synthesis used non-exclusive study-level coding of rainfall, hydrologic-state, response, operational and validation variables. Findings The retained corpus was predominantly railway-direct (83/85). Primary objectives were mechanism/stability response (29), threshold/risk prediction (28), mitigation/rehabilitation (15), monitoring/condition assessment (8) and operational warning/decision (5). Across all studies, stability/failure evidence appeared in 76, infiltration/seepage in 50 and deformation/displacement in 43. Thirty studies contained an explicit operational action, but only 9 of those reported validation, 3 reported non-failure controls, 1 reported a false-alarm metric, 1 a missed-event metric and none reported a lead-time metric. Practical implications For railway infrastructure managers, rainfall thresholds are best treated as network-level screening tools unless route-specific calibration and asset-state information support stronger decisions. Operational studies should report verified non-failure exposure, false alarms, missed events and usable lead time before a threshold, model or sensor output is relied upon for inspection, restriction, closure or resumption. Originality/value This railway-earthw

papers.title: Monitoring Activities on the Devil’s Town Geological Heritage Site, the Republic of Serbia
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: The Devil’s Town (“Đavolja Varoš”) in southern Serbia represents one of the country’s most striking geomorphological landscapes, distinguished by over 200 erosion-sculpted pillars developed within heterogeneous volcaniclastic deposits of the Lece volcanic complex. Earlier pilot research (MEĐA, 2017–2018) demonstrated measurable short-term changes in pillar morphology and slope stability, highlighting the need for systematic monitoring of the site’s dynamic evolution. The DEMONITOR project (2023–2026), funded by the Science Fund of the Republic of Serbia, expands this preliminary work into a comprehensive program integrating advanced remote sensing and geophysical techniques to quantify erosion rates, spatial variability, and process drivers. Focusing on phenomena such as episodic rockfall, subsidence, and surface instability linked to hydro-meteorological agents and material heterogeneity, the project aims to generate predictive assessments of erosion hotspots and scenario-based guidance for conservation planning. As a protected natural monument and UNESCO tentative site, the Devil’s Town provides an important testing ground for developing non-invasive monitoring strategies for fragile geo-heritage. Early results form the basis for improved management recommendations and enhanced understanding of ongoing landscape transformation.

papers.title: A Multi-purpose Large-Scale Laboratory Flume for Gravity-Driven Flows
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: This study introduces a multi-purpose large-scale flume designed to model gravity-driven flows under controlled laboratory conditions. Initially developed for rainfall infiltration and landslide triggering, the facility has been adapted to investigate flow propagation. The set of experiments reported consists of releasing suddenly a large mass (about one-third of a tonne) of granular material onto an inclined plane, varying systematically slope inclination, grain size and substrate roughness. The measurement system of the flume proves particularly well suited to probe the propagation and deposition dynamics of large-scale granular flows. Additionally, the results reveal that slope inclination is a key driver for granular flow mobility, controlling both velocity and deposit morphology, largely surpassing substrate effects. Specifically, flow kinematics is well described by a free-fall-like motion. Building on this observation, we propose a minimal model that accurately predicts flow-front velocity and deposit characteristics—such as runout—from initial conditions including column geometry, frictional angle, and slope inclination. To conclude, this study establishes the flume as a powerful experimental device and provides a robust physical framework for studying gravity-driven flows at large scale, opening the way to future research perspectives.

papers.title: Characterization of the Dynamics of a Landslide System by Means of MT-InSAR Data: The Prototypal Case Study of Torre Orsaia (Cilento Geopark, Southern Italy)
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: Across the Italian territory a lot of historical settlements are threatened by landslide activity. In such cases, effective monitoring strategies are crucial for preserving exposed elements and planning mitigation strategies to reduce the associated risk. In this paper, an approach focused on the integration of conventional surveying and monitoring data, collected by instruments commonly installed in landslide remediation areas, with satellite MT-InSAR data is presented. The test area is the Torre Orsaia village (Campania region, southern Italy), which belongs to the Cilento UNESCO global Geopark. The village has been historically affected by landslides, and over the years several mitigation measures have been adopted. For the purpose of the analysis, the landslide system threatening the village has been described using the LOOM data structure, and the various landslide objects have been kinematically characterized by integrating the object-oriented dataset with interferometric data. The obtained results point out that monitoring data should be carefully contextualized within the hillslope dynamics to address complex settings, such as overlapping landslide types and movements.

papers.title: New Management Board of the ICL Journal “Landslides”: Partnership Publication of the ICL Open Access Book Series “Progress in Landslide Research and Technology”
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: This article introduces the New Management Board of Landslides: Journal of the International Consortium on Landslides. Journal Landslides is the the partnership publication of the ICL Open Access Book Series “Progress in Landslide Research and Technology”. The international journal Landslides was established in April 2004. The Editorial Board of Journal Landslides has included both strictly limited working editors from the Editorial Manager of Landslides, and advisers, managers, promoters including influencers in the field of landslides who are indispensable for the publication of Landslides from March 2004 to March 2026. Based on the requirements from Clarivate, Web of Science et al., the publisher of Landslides—Springer-Verlag requested to move advisers, managers, promoters including influencers in the field of landslides from Editorial Board to other applicable roles. From Vol. 23–4, April 2026, the Editorial Board members are strictly limited to those responsible for editorial decisions on articles of the journal. The Management Board members include advisers, managers and promoters of the Journal.

papers.title: Geospatial Assessment of Rainfall-Triggered Landslide Risk Using Multi-Criteria Decision Techniques in Venezuela
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides are a persistent threat in Venezuela due to a combination of varied topography, tropical rainfall and rapid urbanisation on alluvial fans and unstable hillslopes. This chapter aims to produce national Landslide Risk Index Maps (LRiM) to support disaster reduction initiatives in the country. Multi-Criteria Decision Methods (MCDM), geographic information systems and remote-sensing techniques were used to generate the LRiM, considering hazard, exposure, and vulnerability indicators. Hazard index maps were developed using conditioning factors (i.e., elevation, slope, rainfall, land cover, geology, and proximity to rivers), while the exposure and vulnerability index maps were derived from socio-economic indicators (i.e., population density, building count, proximity to roads, extreme poverty, households with deficits in public services, and inadequate dwellings). Four MCDM were implemented for the modelling purpose: Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Weighted Linear Combination (WLC), Ordered Weighted Average (OWA), and Weighted Overlay (WO). A landslide inventory map with 699 historical rainfall-induced landslides was used to validate the hazard index maps using the area under the curve (AUC) of the receiving operating characteristics (ROC). The AUC values for AHP, WLC, OWA, and WO obtained were 0.891, 0.862, 0.896, and 0.945 respectively.

papers.title: Multi-scale Assessment Procedures of Landslide-Prone Areas via Integrated Analysis of Geo-thematic and Satellite Interferometric Radar Data
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: This paper proposes a multi-scale approach for the assessment of landslide-prone built-up areas by analysing ground deformations through the combined use of satellite interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) data processed by PSI (Persistent Scatterers Interferometry) technique and geomorphological, cartographic, geo-thematic information. The work follows a methodology that encompasses three scales of analysis (small, medium and large), by including some procedures already tested in scientific literature and suitably tailored to the paper aims. The study area is the Tuscany region (Italy) where 20 urban sites are declared “to be consolidated” according to national and regional Building Regulations. At small scale, a PSI-based hotspot analysis is performed over the whole region to identify hotspot built-up areas affected by highest ground deformation rates. At medium scale, the Province of Grosseto is investigated, as characterized by the highest percentage of municipalities affected by hotspot areas. Among them, Roccastrada urban area is selected to carry out detailed analysis at large scale. Historical and recent satellite radar interferometric measurements, in-situ survey and geomorphological assessments are exploited at this stage to examine present and past deformation scenarios, to understand the impacts on urban buildings, as well as to verify the efficiency of consolidation works. Methods and results at regional and provincial scale can support planning activities to create intervention priorities, while outcomes at the urban scale can contribute to improve strategies for managing hydrogeological risk on the built-up fabric.

papers.title: Spectral Element Method-Based Stability Charts for Vegetated Slopes
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: The stability of slopes has long challenged engineers and geologists. While detailed analysis is ideal, it’s not always feasible; slope stability charts offer a practical alternative. Vegetation is a cost-effective solution for stabilizing soil slopes due to its reinforcing properties. This research investigates how the location of vegetation affects soil slope stability using the Spectral Element Method (SEM). Slope models at four angles (26°, 33°, 45°, and 63°) with six vegetation positions are analyzed. Root cohesion and depth simulate vegetation effects. The study calculates critical Strength Reduction Factors (SRFs) for different soil models and validates results against the Finite Element Method (FEM) using Rocscience Phase 2. Sensitivity analysis identifies the most influential vegetation locations. A strong correlation between SEM and FEM confirms the accuracy of the method. The resulting slope stability charts help rapidly evaluate slope safety with respect to vegetation cover location.

papers.title: Multi-source Mapping and Machine Learning Susceptibility Assessment of the 2023 Tuscany Landslides
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: On 2 November 2023, the Tuscany region (central Italy) experienced an extreme rainfall event that triggered numerous shallow, fast-moving landslides in the north-east part. In this study, we map these rainfall-induced landslides using a multi-source approach that integrates high-resolution multispectral optical satellite imagery with detailed field surveys. The resulting event-based landslide inventory is then combined with the regional landslide database to model the spatial susceptibility to shallow, rapid landslides across Tuscany. Landslide susceptibility was modeled using a new generation of interpretable machine learning methods—specifically, Explainable Boosting Machines. The resulting susceptibility map identifies the areas most prone to future shallow, fast-moving landslides and highlights the main predisposing factors contributing to high susceptibility levels. This map represents a valuable tool for land-use planning and risk management and constitutes a key step toward a comprehensive landslide risk assessment for the region.

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Landslides Triggered by the January 2024 Earthquake and the September 2024 Heavy Rainfall in the Noto Peninsula, Japan
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: The M JMA 7.6 earthquake struck the Noto Peninsula, Japan, on 2024 January 1. The powerful earthquake triggered a series of cascading effects, including extensive infrastructure damage, widespread landslides, tsunamis, fire, and liquefaction. This article examines the cascading disasters triggered by the Noto earthquake, focusing on the impacts of landslides. The earthquake triggered more than 2300 landslides. After 9 months, anomalous rainfall in September triggered more than 1540 landslides. This work presents an analysis of spatial patterns, controlling factors, and landslide characteristics triggered by two significant events on the Noto Peninsula, Japan: the January 2024 earthquake and the September 2024 heavy rainfall. Statistical results reveal a shift in susceptibility: while earthquake-induced landslides were concentrated in volcanic units (N1_vas_al), rainfall-induced landslides disproportionately affected sedimentary rocks (sandstone and mudstone (Pg4_sns)), whose failure ratio increased from 15% to 28%. Topographically, both events were highly concentrated at low-to-mid elevations (150–350 m) and moderate-to-steep slopes.

papers.title: Dynamic Graph Neural Network with Adversarial Training for Extreme Landslide Prediction
papers.source: Communications in computer and information science

papers.title: Analysis of the Impacts of Brazil’s Recent Landslide Disaster “Epidemic”
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: In recent times, a growing number of gravitational mass movements (GMMs) of various types has affected Brazil. These events are distributed across several regions of the country and affect both urban and rural areas. In this article, we report the occurrence of approximately 20,000 events over the past 10 years. This extraordinary number of landslides can be framed as a “landslide epidemic”. The impacts of this “epidemic” are examined using data from two disaster databases related to landslides and four reference events, including a road disaster, two regional disasters in southern and southeastern Brazil, and an additional case associated with the rupture of a mining dam in central Brazil. A brief overview of each case study is presented, and its impacts are analyzed in detail. The study presents a comprehensive analysis of disaster impact data on multiple human activities and draws conclusions regarding the characteristics of these hazardous geological processes and the dominant types of impacts observed across the dataset.

papers.title: Implementation of National Guidelines and Strategy on Landslide Risk Management in India: A Review
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: Landslides pose persistent threats to lives, infrastructure and livelihoods in mountainous and geo-dynamically sensitive regions of India, making them a major component of the national disaster risk profile. To address these risks, the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) introduced the National Guidelines on Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches (2009) and the National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019), which collectively emphasize hazard zonation, vulnerability assessment, early warning systems, capacity building and mainstreaming of risk considerations into development planning. This paper reviews the progress and challenges in implementing these frameworks. The Geological Survey of India’s National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping (NLSM), the Landslide Atlas of India by National Remote Sensing Centre, Indian Space Research Organization (NRSC, ISRO) and ongoing meso-scale mapping for critical infrastructure corridors have significantly advanced hazard characterization and exposure assessment. However, operationalization of localized early warning systems, integration of high-resolution susceptibility maps into land-use regulation and systematic application of risk audits in infrastructure projects remain limited. On the other hand, while national guidelines have provided strategic clarity and role allocation, their enforcement across states and sectoral agencies has been uneven, especially in hill-town planning and road development. The review concludes that accelerating meso-scale mapping, establishing standardized protocols for landslide early warning, and embedding susceptibility data into regulatory, financial and planning mechanisms are critical next steps. Strengthening the science policy interface will be key to ensuring that technical advances translate into effective risk reduction and sustainable mountain development.

papers.title: Structural Geology of Rockslide Scarps Analyzed in Virtual Environments to Support Seismic Slope Stability Analysis
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: Geological structures, such as bedding, faults, folds, joints and fractures often contribute to decreased stability of rock slopes according to their strike and dip with respect to the general orientation of the main slope. Additionally, a rock slope may undergo many forms of gravitational displacement-induced (e.g. toppling), erosional (e.g. river undercutting) and/or weathering-induced destabilization. A variety of deep-seated very large (with a volume of > 10 7 m 3) rock slope failures have been analyzed according to their structural characteristics. Studies include field surveys with structural geology measurements and image collection with Unmanned Aerial Vehicles. The latter were then used to construct digital twins of the rockslide sites. Structural elements were analyzed by using stereo-plot tools that can also produce 3D outputs of the studied planes. In a few cases, additional geophysical data were collected in the field (both on the rockslide deposits and on bedrock around the scarps). For some sites, those data were then combined within 3D geomodels of the studied sites and related 3D representations were integrated in immersive virtual environments. To a few models also numerical analyses have been applied. Below, we provide an overview of past studies in the Alps, Carpathians and Tien Shan; including, with more detail, the most recently prospected site of the Karasuu rock avalanche located on the Talas-Fergana Fault in Kyrgyzstan.

papers.title: Coastal—Submarine Landslide Susceptibility Zonation in Palu Bay, Central Sulawesi, Indonesia
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: This study assesses the coastal-submarine landslide susceptibility in Palu Bay using the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), Frequency Ratio (FR), and an integration of AHP–FR. The purpose of this study is to identify areas susceptible to coastal-submarine landslides to support sustainable development in the coastal area of Palu Bay. Six controlling factors—slope gradient, sediment type, Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA), distance from fault, distance from river mouth, and curvature—were analyzed to produce the coastal-submarine landslide susceptibility zonation map. There are four susceptibility zones, namely, low, moderate, high, and very high. Most high to very high-susceptibility zones are located along the coast, and the low to moderate-susceptibility zones are mainly in the central part of Palu Bay. The AHP model has an accuracy of 72.03% (Good); the FR model, 74.42% (Good); and the AHP–FR integration, the highest accuracy of 76.65% (Good). The higher accuracy of the AHP–FR model is due to the combination of expert-based weighting from AHP with data-driven analysis from FR.

papers.title: Repeated Landslides, Gully Erosion and Irrigation: Interactions and Implications for Multi-hazard Management in Northern Ethiopia
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: The Adishu area in northern Ethiopia is a typical example of sites affected by multi-hazards (repeated landslides, gully erosion, siltation) with cascading effects, but where small-scale irrigation, soil and water conservation (SWC), and water harvesting (WH) are practiced. The objective of this study was to evaluate the characteristics and interactions of multi-hazards and recommend mitigation measures. The study (2015–2020) involved: (i) detailed inventory and evaluations of the different cascading hazards, (ii) characterization of the engineering and hydraulic properties of soils and rocks, (iii) assessments of effects of irrigation, SWC, and WH on landslides, (iv) monitoring groundwater levels, soil moisture, spring discharge, and suspended sediment concentration (SSC) in streams/rivers, and (v) recommend multi-hazard mitigation/management options. Debris/earth slides were the main types of landslides, with rockfalls in some areas. The causes for repeated landslides included: (a) presence of higher permeability rock/soil masses at upslope areas (recharge zones), (b) presence of soft and low permeability rocks (Shale) that underlie the unconsolidated sediments, (c) active gully erosion at the lower sections of the slopes, and (d) irrigation, SWC and WH practices which enhance groundwater recharge. SSC was found to be higher (maximum 237.5 g/L) downstream of the landslide-affected areas than upstream (maximum 71.5 g/L). The recommended solutions include: gully treatment (physical and biological); drainage-based water harvesting; improving irrigation water management; and reducing the effects of SWC and WH on landslide initiations. Our findings have important implications for landslide assessments and management, water resources development, and land management in Ethiopia and in other areas with similar conditions.

papers.title: SEM-Based Stability Charts for Varying Ground Water Conditions After Hoek and Bray (1974)
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: Landslides are major natural hazards in mountainous countries like Nepal, often triggered by groundwater through mechanisms such as reduced suction, elevated water tables, and increased pore water pressure. This study develops slope stability charts under varying groundwater conditions using the Spectral Element Method (SEM). Following Hoek and Bray (1974), five groundwater conditions are considered for slope angles of 26°, 33°, 45°, and 63°. Tools like Cubit, Tecplot, Paraview, and the SEM-based program Specfem3D-Geotech are used for modeling and analysis. Stability factors are derived and presented as charts, replacing traditional LEM-based assumptions. Critical Strength Reduction Factors (SRFs), or Factors of Safety (FoS), are identified by plotting maximum displacement versus SRF. The SEM computational procedure follows Tiwari et al. (2013). Validation is performed by comparing SEM-derived charts with Hoek and Bray’s LEM-based failure charts, showing strong correlation and supporting the reliability of the SEM approach.

papers.title: Experimental Study of Pore-Fluid Pressure Dissipation Induced by Debris Flow-Screen Interaction
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: Debris flows in mountainous regions are characterised by their high mobility and significant impact forces, which pose a serious hazard to infrastructure and populations worldwide. Horizontal screens comprising beams aligned in the direction of flow, with fixed openings between them, have been promoted as a cost-effective alternative to traditional vertical barriers. Screens dissipate pore-fluid pressure at the flow-bed interface and reduce flow energy. The pore-fluid pressure dissipation coefficient (R p) has been reported as a key performance indicator, with empirical models relating it to screen design dimensions. However, these models are case- and scale-specific, limiting their use for practical design. This study enhances the understanding of the interactions between debris flow and screen by conducting controlled laboratory experiments using different debris-flow types, from dilute to dense flows. The experimental results show that R p decreases as the normalised pore-fluid pressure increases, underscoring the critical influence of debris-flow type on pore-fluid pressure dissipation and screen performance. Dilute flows are demonstrated to generate positive excess pore pressure, while dense flows tend to produce negative excess pore pressure. R p is shown to be underestimated by existing empirical models. Therefore, a universal theoretical model is needed to predict pore-fluid pressure dissipation induced by flow-screen interactions for a wide range of debris-flow types, enabling systematic field design of screens.

papers.title: Landslide Volume Calculation Using GIS and UAVs
papers.source: Progress in landslide research and technology
papers.summary: Worldwide, landslides pose a major natural hazard, with potentially catastrophic consequences for human life and their socio-economic activities. A rapid assessment of landslide hazards is essential for pre- and post-disaster decision-making. However, a significant limitation is monitoring landslides over the short term. Unmanned aerial vehicles have rapidly emerged as a new tool for local-scale landslide monitoring. Studies have benefited from their high-resolution products, such as digital surface models, digital elevation models, and orthophotos. These products are very useful for modeling and estimating landslide volumes. This paper provides an overview of an ongoing research project from the International Landslide Program (IPL #281) in collaboration the Institute of Geography at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) that seeks to analyze the distribution of landslides and its volumes along stream systems of Iztaccíhuatl volcano, Mexico. The Río Xopanac within the Apizato-Xopanac watershed on the eastern flank of Iztaccíhuatl is selected as a case study. The study demonstrates the use of unmanned aerial vehicles as a tool for monitoring visible changes in landslides volume in remote, mountainous, and difficult-to-access areas. We implement a volume model in a Geographic Information System that allows for the evaluation of the dynamics of landslide activity. The shallow-slide type of landslide was selected, and the area and volume of representative individual landslides were used to establish an empirical relationship of area-volume that takes the form of a power law. The relationship was used to estimate the total volume of landslides in the study area. The study shows that shallow landslides here have the potential to deliver ~ 126,000 m 3 of sediments to the river. The findings are important in understanding the long-term volume of landslides along the stream system on the eastern flank of Iztaccihuatl.

papers.title: Peta Evakuasi Partisipatif Berbasis Analisis Spasial Space Syntax di Desa Sibetan
papers.summary: Sibetan Village, Bebandem District, Karangasem Regency, is a snake fruit (Salak) agrotourism area located within Mount Agung’s Disaster-Prone Area (KRB) II, making it vulnerable to pyroclastic flows, lava flows, lahars, and landslides. The Banjar Dukuh community faces limited disaster mitigation knowledge and evacuation route awareness, compounded by the absence of evacuation maps and signage. This Community Service (PKM) activity aimed to strengthen community preparedness through disaster mitigation education and participatory evacuation mapping. A participatory action research approach was implemented through five stages: observation and data collection, interviews and focus group discussions (FGDs), spatial analysis, evacuation mapping and signage recommendations, and socialization and evacuation simulation. The activity involved 20 participants, comprising 15 residents, three village officials, and two Pasebaya members, alongside two FGD sessions involving 25 participants. Pre-test and post-test results showed an increase in average community understanding scores from 65 to 85, representing a 30.7% improvement. The activity produced a validated evacuation map identifying four assembly points, four evacuation routes, and four recommended signage locations. These outcomes strengthened community preparedness, self-reliance, and village institutional capacity while enhancing applied learning for Architecture students and supporting Universitas Warmadewa’s Key Performance Indicators (IKU).

papers.title: Project management in emergency slope stabilization works: the Estrada da Graciosa case (PR-410, Morretes, Paraná)
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Between November 2022 and February 2023, intense rainfall in the Serra do Mar mountain rangetriggered landslides at six locations along the Estrada da Graciosa (PR-410), a historic road inMorretes, Paraná, Brazil, damaging slopes both above and below the roadway and forcing roadclosures. The Paraná State Highway Department (DER/PR) awarded an emergency design-and-buildcontract for slope stabilization (Contract No. 014/2023, initial value of BRL 39.0 million). Fieldworks were completed in December 2023, and the contract was closed in February 2024. This paperexamines the case from a project management perspective, drawing on the seven performancedomains and six principles of the PMBOK® Guide – Eighth Edition and on the ConstructionExtension to the PMBOK® Guide. It describes the geotechnical solutions adopted (anchored wallsover jet-grouting columns, vegetated soil nailing, shotcrete facing and deep horizontal drains) and themanagement method applied: an integrated system for managing execution, productivity and contractperformance, combined with a per-site critical cycle and a monthly measurement routine. The resultsshow that the method made it possible to run five simultaneous work fronts while keeping the roadopen, to limit the only scheduled full closure to three days, and to close the contract with fullyreconciled measurements. The paper argues that, on roads that sustain a regional economy, thequality of project management determines how long traffic is restricted. Its effects therefore reachbeyond the client and the contractor, to local businesses and tourism, to public administration and tothe construction sector. The article also discusses the relevance of these practices to publicemergency infrastructure recovery programs, such as the Federal Highway Administration'sEmergency Relief program in the United States, where oversight bodies have identified thedocumentation of decisions as a weak point.

papers.title: Conditional generative adversarial networks for degraded image enhancement and synthetic data generation in landslide crack detection and quantification
papers.summary: This study proposes an integrated framework for landslide crack detection and dimension estimation by combining conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs), deep learning-based segmentation, and image processing techniques. The cGAN models were employed to enhance synthetically degraded unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images under simulated low-light, overexposure, and cloud-obscuration conditions and to generate synthetic images for data augmentation. Five U-Net models with different encoder backbones were evaluated for crack segmentation, while image processing techniques were applied to estimate crack length and width. The cGAN-based image enhancement achieved structural similarity index (SSIM) values of 0.77–0.93 and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) values of 25.39–31.64 dB. Image enhancement improved crack segmentation performance across all three simulated degradation conditions, with F1 scores increasing from 0.195–0.810 to 0.692–0.865. Incorporating cGAN-generated synthetic images into the training dataset further improved F1 scores by 1.1–5.8%, with VGG16 achieving the highest F1 score of 0.871. The relative errors in estimated crack length and width, calculated against manually annotated reference masks, ranged from 3.8% to 11.65%. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework to improve landslide crack detection and dimension estimation under simulated adverse imaging conditions, supporting its further development for UAV-based landslide monitoring and assessment.

papers.summary: 该数据集提供了来自中国新疆新疆一处露天煤矿南侧高墙及内部倾倒坡密集监测网络的带标记微震和运行振动波形。它发布用于事件检测、多类别分类、信号特性分析以及在实际采矿噪声下的类别失衡感知评估。档案分为四个文件夹和一个目录指南。该文件夹分类事件级波形数据/包含标记为10秒垂直分量的.npy记录，分为五个本地类别文件夹：微震/（微震事件）、爆破/（爆破）、small_landslide/（小型滑坡）、mechanical_mining/（机械采矿）和transport_vehicles/（运输车辆）。文件夹原始波形数据/提供了2025年6月1日的连续miniSEED示例，用于复现预处理和检测过程。文件夹站元数据/存储传感器位置（内部倾倒坡度）.xlsx传感器位置（南部高墙）.xlsx。文件夹数据日志/包括可用性工作簿（data_20250601_20250720.xls、data_20250601.xlsx）、每日类别计数以及训练/验证/测试拆分摘要（event_counts_20250601_20250720.xlsx）、五类事件关联表（five_class_event_catalog.csv、waveform_to_event_id.csv和blasting_station_count_distribution.csv），以及 station-inventory.xml。文件目录documentation.txt总结了目录结构。文档、站点元数据和数据日志会与大型波形包分开上传，用户可以在下载完整卷之前检查内容。

Smart Emergency Communication System for Natural Disasters using LoRa
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Natural disasters such as floods, earthquakes, cyclones, and landslides can disrupt conventional communication infrastructure, making it difficult for affected individuals to communicate during emergencies. This paper presents a Smart Emergency Communication System for Natural Disasters Using Long Range (LoRa) technology. The proposed system consists of transmitter and receiver units implemented using ESP32 development boards and SX1278 LoRa modules operating at 433 MHz. A smartphone is connected to the transmitter through Bluetooth to send text messages, which are transmitted wirelessly to the receiver using LoRa. A panic button is integrated into the transmitter to initiate an emergency alert containing Global Positioning System (GPS) coordinates when a valid location fix is available. At the receiver, the received messages and emergency alerts are displayed on a 16 × 2 liquid crystal display (LCD). Experimental testing demonstrated communication over a distance of up to 2 km in a built-up environment with obstacles. The GPS module provided valid coordinates in open spaces; however, in closed spaces, valid coordinates could not be obtained, resulting in zero coordinates being included in the panic alert. The developed prototype demonstrates the feasibility of LoRa-based emergency messaging without relying on cellular networks or internet connectivity for the direct transmitter-to-receiver link. The system can serve as a supplementary communication solution for disaster-affected and remote areas.

papers.title: A time-decaying strength-legacy model for post-seismic rainfall thresholds, illustrated with a Kaikoura recovery timescale
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Large earthquakes weaken slopes, and failures often follow months to years later, in rainfall harmless before the earthquake. This paper models that delay with an infinite-slope factor of safety and transient infiltration (Iverson, 2000), with a legacy factor fs(t) = 1 - Delta exp(-t/tau) on strength. Tau = 1.69 years follows from Cao et al. (2023): 21 large Kaikoura landslides lost 90% of post-seismic velocity in a mean of 3.9 years. Delta is solved from published threshold drops: 0.059 for the Wenchuan drop of 15-22%, and 0.220 for the Chi-Chi drop of 83.2% (867 to 146 mm); central Delta = 0.140 is their mean. On an idealised slope (FoS_dry = 1.340, intact critical rainfall 518 mm/48 h), the central case gives 270 mm immediately after the earthquake, 390 mm at 1 year and 497 mm at 3.9 years. Monte Carlo (N = 5000) censored medians are 691 mm intact and 226 mm damaged; 25.0% of intact versus 46.7% of damaged slopes fail in a 183 mm/48 h storm. A calibration exercise on an idealised slope, not a site-specific validation.

papers.title: Array-Informed Landslide Localization in Sparse Seismic Networks: Application to the Nepal Himalaya
papers.summary: In August and October 2026, two massive mass movements and associated destructive flash floods occurred in the Nepal Himalaya. These events highlight the growing importance of rapid seismic detection and localization of hazardous slope failures in mountainous regions. However, sparse and uneven seismic networks often result in large localization errors, particularly in remote, under-instrumented regions. We investigate how well a compact seismic array increases the resilience of landslide localization under sparse network conditions. We combine array-derived back azimuths with regional wave-arrival times for the 26 August 2026 Tsangbu Ri and 10 October 2026 Budhi-Gandaki events in Nepal. A group of Raspberry Shake seismometers near Kathmandu, not originally designed as an array, accurately recovers back-azimuths for both events. Combining these directional constraints with arrival times from only a few regional stations yields localization precision comparable to conventional localization using the distributed Nepal School Seismology Network along with other public stations. Progressive station-removal tests confirm that array-informed localization generally maintains lower errors and more stable solutions as network coverage decreases. Hence, compact seismic arrays may provide a robust and practical tool for monitoring remote landslides where seismic networks are sparse, data access is limited, or sustainable station maintenance is difficult and costly.

papers.title: Rock-bridge resistance and failure modes are controlled by ligament stress paths
papers.summary: Natural joints and faults are often not fully continuous, characterised by rock bridges to interrupt joint and fault connections. Geomechanical studies have indicated that the resistance behaviours of rock bridges against connections across field and lab scales are highly complex, thereby remaining conceptual and beyond deterministic analysis. Here we show that the resistance and failure modes of rock bridges are controlled by stress paths on ligaments. Laboratory tests on notched sandstones validate theoretical predictions of the resistance and failure modes, both of which show stress-orientation dependence. Moreover, we apply the theory to a rockslide and a fault hard-linkage case, facilitating landslide early warning and fault-linkage/seismogenic-potential assessment.

papers.title: Numerical evaluation of seismic interferometry for monitoring rainfall-induced shear-wave velocity changes in sandy soils
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides pose a persistent threat to tropical urban slopes, where the absence of physically grounded monitoring systems severely constrains early warning capabilities. This paper presents and implements an integrated numerical chain that links water infiltration to an observable seismic signal using a physics-informed framework that couples standard hydraulic and elastic parameters rather than site-calibrated empirical thresholds: the Richards equation with van Genuchten–Mualem parameterization governs wetting-front advance; Gassmann fluid substitution translates time-varying saturation profiles into elastic models, predicting a −10.6% reduction in V S ( 614 → 549 m/s ) between the dry and fully saturated states; and two independent wave propagation codes—FDELMODC (finite differences) and SPECFEM2D (spectral elements)—generate synthetic seismograms at six infiltration snapshots (1–20 h) under both active-source and passive ambient-noise configurations. The stretching method gives total d v / v variations of the same order across codes: | Δ | = 1.05 % and 1.06% under active acquisition, and | Δ | = 1.06 % and 0.77% under passive monitoring, although the passive estimates depend on the processing choices. A complementary F-K dispersion inversion recovers Δ V S / V S values between −10 and −12% in the near-surface layer, consistent with the Gassmann theoretical prediction of −10.6%. The study provides a numerical basis for developing and testing the method; further work is needed to reduce the dependence of the passive estimates on the processing choices before comparison with field data.

papers.title: Integrated Hydrogeological Assessment of Underground Constructions in Swelling-Prone Keuper Lithologies: Insights from the Markusberg Tunnel (Luxembourg)
papers.summary: The construction and long-term stability of underground structures in swelling-prone lithologies pose geotechnical challenges, particularly in clay–sulfate Keuper formations. This study presents an integrated, multi-scale hydrogeological assessment of the Markusberg Tunnel (Luxembourg), a twin-tube highway tunnel affected by severe syn- and post-construction deformation and heave in clay–sulfate-rich Keuper lithology. The investigation combines hydrogeological, geological, construction-related, and geomorphological analyses to identify the mechanisms controlling swelling and associated heave. Hydrochemical analyses, drainage discharge monitoring, and mixing calculations reveal the intrusion of multiple groundwater types, including meteoric and highly saline artesian waters, into the tunnel near-field and associated excavation damage zone (EDZ), potentially contributing to ongoing heave through clay swelling, sulfate dissolution, and gypsum precipitation. Structural-geological mapping, LiDAR-based geomorphological analyses, and field surveys identified landslides near the tunnel alignment that may act as preferential infiltration pathways into low-permeability Keuper formations. The results suggest that tunnel excavation may have established a hydraulic short circuit between weathered and unweathered sulfate rocks, promoting sustained expansive reactions, local karstification, and long-term deformation. Persistent swelling points to an open hydrogeological system that enables continuous groundwater circulation and water–rock interaction in the tunnel surroundings. These findings underline the importance of multidisciplinary, multi-scale site investigations to resolve system behavior and develop effective monitoring and mitigation strategies for underground construction in swelling-prone formations.

Review article: From spatial to spatial-temporal rainfall representation and beyond in landslide susceptibility modelling
papers.summary: Rainfall is increasingly incorporated as a time-dependent predictor in landslide susceptibility modelling, yet its temporal evolution is rarely preserved. Instead, rainfall is commonly condensed into scalar statistical descriptors, limiting how rainfall-triggering processes are represented and learned. This review synthesizes 211 studies published between 2000 and 2025 that explicitly incorporate time-varying rainfall information into landslide susceptibility modelling. The review reveals that the apparent importance of rainfall often depends on how spatial heterogeneity and temporal variability are represented within susceptibility models. At regional scales, broad terrain–climate heterogeneity can amplify the statistical importance attributed to rainfall. Beyond the temporal attribution uncertainty introduced by spatial presence–absence sampling, rainfall evolution is predominantly reduced to scalar descriptors that provide a lossy representation of rainfall processes: selected characteristics are retained, while temporal organization and potentially triggering-relevant rainfall patterns are discarded before entering the model. Looking forward, intensifying hydroclimate volatility under climate change makes the temporal organization of rainfall increasingly critical for understanding rainfall-triggered landslides. At the same time, advances in high-resolution data and sequence learning make it feasible to move beyond scalar rainfall descriptors and learn complete rainfall patterns from their temporal evolution, paving the way towards more process-informed prediction of rainfall-triggered landslides.

papers.title: Spatially Cross-Validated Machine Learning for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping on the Unstable Slopes of the Tellian Atlas: Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Machines (Azazga, Northern Algeria)
papers.summary: Random splits of autocorrelated pixels place test points within metres of training data. Random forest, XGBoost, and support vector machines were trained on 15 predisposing factors and 45,900 pixels of a field-validated inventory of 24 landslide bodies (Azazga) and evaluated on five folds of 500 m blocks (autocorrelation range 497 m) with a 100 m buffer. The spatial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.693, 0.702, and 0.749—conservative relative to a random split (0.995 for the random forest) but not fully independent of the inventory’s spatial structure—and 0.668–0.695 with each body confined to one fold. The default radial-basis support vector machine ranked first in the main analysis and in 13 sensitivity configurations, by margins (0.011–0.053) mostly unresolved; nested tuning brought no external gain. Lithology alone reached 0.686 (0.665 with the original geological map; 0.620, models 0.611–0.660, after removing the main landslide deposits merged into the scree unit); terrain derivatives recomputed from Copernicus elevation data gained weight. Only the highest class was separated from the next in every model. At equal area, model agreement captured no more landslide area than the support vector machine (29.6% against 29.8%): an uncertainty layer beside a map refitted on all data.

papers.title: Post-fire shallow landslide susceptibility and hazard assessment following recurrent wildfires in Western Greece
papers.summary: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for assessing shallow landslide susceptibility and hazard in post-wildfire environments. The methodology combines the Frequency Ratio (FR) bivariate statistical model for spatial susceptibility mapping with annual probability estimations of landslide triggering across a repeatedly burned region in Western Greece. The empirical data set encompasses shallow landslide occurrences documented following multiple fire events between 2007 and 2024. Most mapped instabilities correspond to reactivations of pre-existing landslide deposits, driven by intense or prolonged rainfall during post-fire seasons. Quantitative analysis demonstrates that post-fire shallow slope failures in the study area exhibit a maximum annual activation probability of approximately 35 %, corresponding to a minimum recurrence interval of roughly 2.9 years (1/0.35 ≃ 2.86 years). This research clarifies the role of key predisposing environmental drivers in controlling the spatial distribution, magnitude, and movement mechanisms of post-fire slope failures. The resulting dynamic models offer actionable decision-support tools for disaster risk reduction, land-use planning, and early warning strategies in fire-prone regions.

papers.title: Extractive Industries and their Impact on Ecosystems and Historical Sites: Case of Georgia
papers.summary: This article examines the environmental and cultural impacts of extractive industries in Georgia, focusing on their effects on ecosystems, water resources, biodiversity, landscapes, local communities, and historical heritage. Particular attention is given to major mining regions, including Bolnisi/Madneuli and Chiatura, as well as the Sakdrisi-Kachagiani archaeological complex, recognized as one of the world’s oldest known gold-mining sites. The study employs a qualitative analytical approach based on comparative examination of existing research, statistical data, institutional reports, and documented cases of environmental and cultural degradation. The analysis demonstrates that intensive extraction of manganese, copper, and gold has contributed to soil erosion, water and air pollution, heavy-metal contamination, habitat degradation, landslides, and landscape transformation. The study also highlights the destruction and endangerment of historical and archaeological heritage associated with mining activities. Particular emphasis is placed on weaknesses in environmental regulation, insufficient monitoring, limited communication between government institutions, mining companies, and local communities, and the prioritization of short-term economic interests over long-term environmental protection. The findings indicate that although extractive industries contribute to employment, industrial production, and exports, their environmental and social costs require stronger regulatory oversight and more effective environmental governance. The article emphasizes the need for integrated sustainable resource management that combines ecological conservation, community interests, and cultural heritage protection.
