Bypassed Oil Recovery in High-Temperature, High-Salinity Heterogeneous Carbonate Reservoirs by Aqueous Ketone Solution
papers.summary: Recent studies have shown that 3-pentanone remains aqueous-stable and non-emulsifying while altering wettability under extremely harsh reservoir conditions (e.g., 372.15 K and 200,000 ppm). This study investigates bypassed-oil recovery using aqueous 3-pentanone in heterogeneous carbonate rock under high-temperature, high-salinity (HTHS) conditions, with an emphasis on how preferential flow affects the ketone’s phase partitioning, in situ accumulation, and convective oil displacement. A spontaneous imbibition (SI) experiment was first conducted using formation brine (FB: 224,358 ppm), sulfate-rich injection brine (IB: 54,471 ppm), and 1.1 wt % 3-pentanone in IB (3pIB) to evaluate 3-pentanone-induced wettability alteration and oil recovery from bypassed regions. Corefloods were then performed by injecting 3-pentanone at its aqueous solubility limit in FB (0.3 wt %) and IB (1.1 wt %) under secondary and tertiary flooding conditions in carbonate cores selected to represent preferential-flow behavior. The SI experiment showed that 3-pentanone enhanced capillary-driven imbibition and recovered additional oil beyond that achieved with IB alone. In corefloods, IB and 3pIB injections improved oil recovery relative to FB injection. Material-balance analysis showed that preferential flow accelerated 3-pentanone breakthrough to 0.27 PVI, compared with the 1.92 PVI predicted by the analytical solution, and delayed in situ ketone accumulation. Nevertheless, the high K-value of 3-pentanone enabled continued partitioning into unswept regions. The early ketone breakthrough and effluent pH response indicate that preferential flow generated bypassed regions where salinity gradients between injected and resident brines promoted the release of 3-pentanone from the aqueous phase and its transport into these bypassed regions, thereby facilitating wettability alteration and additional oil recovery.

papers.title: Assessing the use of borehole magnetic resonance (BMR) in conjunction with packer testing to estimate hydraulic conductivity in fractured rock
papers.summary: Collecting appropriate field data to characterize hydraulic conductivity is critical to estimating pore pressure and its impact on rock mass stability in open pit and underground mines. This study aims to explore the applicability, challenges, and limitations of estimating hydraulic conductivity from borehole magnetic resonance (BMR) surveys in fractured rock mass undertaken during geotechnical and hydrogeological drilling programs. Although BMR is frequently used to assess hydraulic properties in sedimentary environments, there has been limited investigation in fractured rock masses, where permeability is governed by the presence and interconnectivity of fractures rather than matrix porosity. This study assesses the benefits and limitations of existing empirical methods for deriving hydraulic conductivity estimates from BMR data in fractured rock and compares hydraulic conductivity estimates from BMR survey data to packer testing results. This case study uses data from a single site, where a combination of BMR downhole surveys and packer tests in selected boreholes and intervals were conducted to obtain representative hydraulic conductivity within the rock mass and major structure.

papers.title: Prioritizing Fuel Treatments to Reduce Post-Fire Debris Flow Risk in Utah
papers.summary: Wildfire is a natural part of many forest ecosystems, but in the western United States, wildfires have become larger, more frequent, and more severe in recent decades. There are serious problems after severe wildfire, including erosion, flooding, and debris flows that threaten water quality, roads, and communities. Because of this, land managers need better ways to decide where fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning or thinning, can most effectively reduce wildfire damage and post-fire risks. In this dissertation, I studied how fuel treatments might reduce wildfire severity and lower the risk of post-fire debris flows in Utah. First, I built a model to predict how severely forests are likely to burn across the state. Next, I used simulated treatment scenarios to test how different fuel treatments changed wildfire severity in different forest types and under different weather conditions. Finally, I applied those results to real watersheds in Utah to estimate how treatments could reduce post-fire debris-flow risk. The results showed that treatment effectiveness depends strongly on forest type. In some forests, especially ponderosa pine, spruce-fir, and lodgepole pine, reducing fuels had a strong effect on lowering fire severity. In other forest types, weather played a larger role, which made treatments less effective. Across most forests, treatments that reduced both canopy fuels and surface fuels produced the greatest reductions in wildfire severity. At the watershed scale, treatment costs and benefits also varied. Prescribed burning was generally the most cost-effective treatment. In several watersheds, including Electric Lake, Big Cottonwood Canyon, Panguitch Lake, and Rockport, cost-effective treatments provided the greatest reduction in post-fire risk for the money invested, making them especially important areas for management. Other watersheds showed less cost-benefit tradeoffs in decision making, where intensive treatments can be prioritized for maximal b

Cascading natural and socioeconomic impacts of Canadian wildfires
papers.summary: Wildfires alter the physical, chemical, and biological properties of ecosystems, potentially triggering cascading natural and socioeconomic consequences within burned areas and in surrounding (downstream/downslope) unburned environments. In particular, fire-induced changes to forested watersheds can significantly increase runoff and erosion rates, enhancing the risk of hazardous flooding and/or debris flows. In response to recent increases in wildfire activity, southwestern Canada is now experiencing post-fire debris flows at frequencies comparable to, or possibly even exceeding, those observed in California. The subsequent transport of sediment and pollutants from burned areas into downstream aquatic environments can degrade water quality by increasing turbidity and altering water chemistry. When these processes occur near drinking-water supply areas, they can compromise the provision of safe drinking water, potentially necessitating costly treatment. Furthermore, evacuations may be necessary during wildfires, or afterwards because of geohazard risks, causing short- and long-term distress among evacuees. In addition to the direct costs and impacts related to wildfire, further economic costs are incurred in the post-fire interval, including those related to cascading post-fire natural hazard impacts, landscape rehabilitation, and risk reduction. The scope, scale, and duration of cascading impacts from wildfire underscore the necessity for research, rapid assessment and monitoring programs, and rehabilitation strategies to protect the health and safety of Canadian communities and ecosystems.

papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This dataset and accompanying Python code reproduce Figure 1e of the manuscript “Closing the gap between Experimental and Natural Debris Flows with the World's Largest Flume.” The Excel workbook contains 1,490 compiled records across 84 source labels, comprising 1,163 physical-model experiment records and 327 field-monitoring records. It includes the physical inputs used in the scaling analysis, the pore fluid pressure number (NP), the quasi-Reynolds number (NR), and the flow volume used to scale the plotted markers. One field record with zero volume is retained in the workbook and excluded from the plot, yielding 1,489 plotted records. The accompanying scripts and README provide the files and instructions needed to regenerate the figure in PNG and PDF formats.

papers.title: Historical evidence that wildfire frequency modulates debris-flow hazards through sediment-supply limitation
papers.summary: Southern California is an epicenter of postwildfire debris flows. In this region, steep topography, frequent fire, heavy rainstorms, and large populations along the wildland-urban interface conspire to produce costly debris flows. Wildfire frequency in the region has tripled in recent decades, causing concern about escalating debris-flow hazards. Here, we investigate how wildfire frequency affects the magnitude of postfire erosion by analyzing long-term debris basin records. We identify two contrasting erosional styles. In steep catchments, erosion exhibits a binge-purge behavior: Erosion for 3 years following fire exceeds background rates by ∼17×. In contrast, in low-sloping, soil-mantled catchments, sediment export following fire only exceeds background rates by ∼1.5×. Critically, in the steep catchments, debris-flow volumes decline when wildfires recur more frequently than the ∼30-year interval characteristic of the past century. This observation suggests a sediment-supply limitation in which more frequent wildfire may reduce, rather than amplify, some of Southern California's most severe debris-flow hazards.

papers.title: Predicting soil-water characteristic curve evolution using pore-scale modelling approach
papers.source: Journal of Natural and Agricultural Sciences
papers.summary: Soils in construction are difficult to predict due to their deformability and complex composition. In unsaturated states, suction from air–water interfaces controls hydro-mechanical behavior by influencing interparticle forces. Environmental changes modify suction and cause shrinkage or expansion. The soil-water characteristic curve links suction and saturation, improving constitutive models and enabling better prediction of soil response under varying conditions.

papers.title: Bio-based Methods to Stabilise Problematic Soils: Application to Infrastructure Earthworks.
papers.source: CINECA IRIS Institutial Research Information System (University of Genoa)
papers.summary: Infrastructure earthworks require soils with adequate strength, manageable deformation and suitable hydraulic behaviour. Conventional stabilisation with cement and lime can achieve these requirements, but their manufacture has substantial negative environmental effects. Biopolymers offer a potential means of reducing reliance on conventional binders, but their performance is often assessed through strength tests under partially saturated conditions. Their behaviour in saturated and/or near-saturated conditions, effects on compressibility and drainage, and the benefits of combining them with a traditional stabiliser like hydrated lime remain insufficiently understood. This study addresses these gaps to establish when biopolymer-hydrated lime treatment can provide useful soil improvement. An experimental programme investigated London clay, Ligurian sandy silt, pyroclastic silty sand and Karlsruhe fine sand. Treatment of these soils with Guar gum (GG), xanthan gum (XG) and agar gum (AG) was examined either alone or as partial replacements for hydrated lime (HL), at a fixed total stabiliser content of 3% of dry soil mass. Atterberg limits and standard Proctor tests characterised London clay consistency and compaction; oedometer, evaporation and direct shear tests examined the hydromechanical responses of the coarser soils. Saturated consolidated drained triaxial tests further assessed untreated, HL-treated and AG-containing Karlsruhe fine sand under effective confining stresses of 100, 300 and 600 kPa. In London clay, GG markedly increased the liquid limit, while XG produced a non-monotonic response with the highest liquid limit at 2%HL–1%XG. AG caused comparatively small liquid-limit changes. HL and GG had only a marginal effect on standard Proctor compaction characteristics. These contrasting responses show that changes in soil consistency do not necessarily imply equivalent changes in compactability and that biopolymer type and mixture composition govern treatment be

papers.title: Disentangling Sources of Uncertainty in Modeling Saltwater Intrusion Due To Sea Level Rise: The Effects of Model Dimensionality, Physics, and Parameter Choice
papers.summary: In coastal aquifers, saltwater intrusion driven by rising sea levels threatens agriculture, ecosystems, and underground infrastructure. Quantifying this process requires numerous modeling decisions that introduce uncertainties; however, most studies only quantify uncertainty due to parameter choices once a modeling approach has been selected. Our goal was to evaluate uncertainties arising from both model and parameter choice when estimating freshwater–saltwater interface movement in response to 1 m of sea‐level rise and various changes in groundwater recharge. We compare four modeling approaches applied to one synthetic coastal landscape with homogeneous (but uncertain) hydraulic properties: a 1D + Analytical sharp‐interface solution, quasi‐2D and quasi‐3D sharp‐interface models, and a 2D variable‐density flow and salt transport model. All numerical models were constructed in MODFLOW 6. Parameter and model‐choice uncertainty were calculated using a Moment‐Based Global Sensitivity Analysis of interface movement at a centroid cross‐section of the coastal watershed. Results indicate that hydraulic conductivity is the dominant source of uncertainty under reduced recharge conditions, followed by aquifer thickness, while the model approach becomes more pronounced under constant or increasing recharge scenarios. These findings highlight the importance of constraining hydraulic conductivity to improve saltwater intrusion predictions. Furthermore, 1D and 2D approaches are limited in capturing out‐of‐plane and regional flow processes represented in 3D models, and simplified 1D + Analytical models reach full intrusion at lower combined hydraulic conductivity and recharge values than density‐dependent models. This study provides guidance for evaluating saltwater intrusion across various modeling frameworks applicable to other coastal watersheds.

papers.title: Before PFAS arrive: the native charge of the air–water interface sets trace PFOA adsorption and its response to salt
papers.summary: (PFAS) in unsaturated soils and their removal by foam fractionation, but how salt and pH change it at environmental concentrations (ng L−1 to µg L−1) is not established. The two descriptions in use were built from surface tension at mg L−1 and above. In one, adsorbed PFAS alone charge the interface, which predicts no salt effect at trace level. In the other, adsorption requires counter-ion pairing with a constant exponent, which predicts the same power law at every concentration. I show that neither carries to trace concentrations, and I develop a third description in which the bare air–water interface carries its own regulated negative charge and a trace PFAS anion responds only to its screened potential. The native charge is described by two closures, hydroxide bound to sparse sites and nanomolar surface-active impurities, with a screened image-charge correction. Calibrated on bubble zeta potentials alone (49 observations from five laboratories) and with one fitted constant for perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), the hydroxide closure describes column transport coefficients with AICc 14.3 to 17.0, against 20.3 for self-charging and 109 for mass action, and predicts without refitting the higher adsorption at lower pH. A single fitted surface charge accounts for the eight-fold rise of PFOA adsorption on foam bubbles between 0.5 and 10 mM NaCl. Against eight adsorption coefficients from four further studies it gives a log correlation of 0.82 and a typical error of a factor of 3.1. The largest misses are all on one side: at about 0.1 M salt, with calcium at high coverage, and with co-surfactants, three independent methods place PFOA adsorption above the ceiling that any negative interface allows. I state predictions for a bubble experiment at two pH values that separates the descriptions and the two closures.

papers.title: Beyond BET Surface Area: Accessible Porosity and Interfacial Binding Govern Batch and Fixed-Bed Phenol Capture by Porous Carbons
papers.summary: The rational design of carbonaceous adsorbents for organic pollutant remediation requires moving beyond surface-area-centric metrics toward understanding carbon–water interfacial thermodynamics and structural accessibility. In this work, KOH-activated rice straw biochars (KRBCs) were developed via controlled KOH activation to systematically elucidate the mechanistic balance between pore structure, surface functionalities, and phenol (PhOH) uptake capacity. The moderately activated carbon (KRBC-2) demonstrated superior performance with an ultrafast adsorption equilibrium achieved within 10 min and a maximum Langmuir capacity of 164.008 mg·g–1 at 298 K. Intriguingly, overactivated carbon with higher BET surface area displayed inferior kinetic uptake, proving that accessible porosity and carbon-skeleton integrity─rather than raw surface area─dominate interfacial mass transport and site availability. Reversibility and thermodynamic studies demonstrated that PhOH sorption was spontaneous, exothermic, and highly sustainable (>90% efficiency after consecutive regeneration cycles). XPS and DFT calculations comprehensively revealed that the adsorption is driven by a multimodal mechanism: planar graphitic domains and nanoconfined pores induce strong π–π electron donor–acceptor and dispersion stabilization, whereas oxygen-containing polar sites contribute supplemental hydrogen bonding and local charge polarization. Overall, this study establishes a quantitative, experimentally constrained picture of PhOH adsorption at porous carbon interfaces, highlighting that moderate KOH activation optimizes pollutant accessibility while avoiding structural overdestruction.

papers.title: Multi-Objective Design of Combined Drainage Systems in Homogeneous Earth Dams Using Finite-Element, Pareto, and TOPSIS Methods
papers.summary: Internal drainage in earth dams must improve downstream stability without causing unnecessary seepage discharge. A coupled finite-element framework was developed for the design of a horizontal blanket connected to a downstream toe drain in homogeneous earth dams. Three embankment heights (15, 25, 35 m) and two downstream slopes (1V:1.5H, 1V:2H) were analysed in ABAQUS under steady-state seepage. Design variables were the normalized blanket length (d/N), toe-drain height ratio (h/H) and blanket thickness (b). The downstream factor of safety (FOS) was obtained by strength reduction, and Q is the steady-state seepage discharge per unit width. Simulated designs were ranked by fast non-dominated sorting and crowding distance (NSGA-II framework), and the Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) selected a compromise solution from the non-dominated set. Grey Wolf Optimizer-tuned Random Forest surrogates served only for a within-boundary consistency check. The ratio h/H was the strongest control on FOS: raising it from 0.10 to 0.30 increased FOS by up to about 24% for short blankets, whereas the response to blanket length diminished beyond d/N ≈ 0.4–0.5. A 2.5-fold increase in blanket thickness changed FOS by only about 2.1%. The Pareto sets concentrated near d/N = 0.50–0.60 and h/H = 0.25–0.30 for the 25 and 35 m dams, while the 15 m cases spanned h/H = 0.10–0.30. The surrogates reproduced FOS better than Q (weakest case: Q for 35 m, 1V:1.5H, testing R² = 0.46). The resulting ranges are preliminary, model-specific design bands rather than universal optima.

The repository contains the soil hydraulic properties (HYPROP), the plant and soil measurements of both campaigns, and the Python scripts that derive transpiration downregulation thresholds on the scales of soil water content, matric potential, unsaturated hydraulic conductivity K(h) and matric flux potential, and that produce the statistics, figures and tables of the article. See README for the layout and how to run the scripts.

papers.title: Model-derived uncertainty bounds for unsaturated hydraulic conductivity in artificially structured (ASD) residual soils
papers.summary: Given that soil - water characteristic curves (SWCC) measurements are time-consuming and costly, researchers are focusing on equations and reasonable variations in the fitting parameters to estimate SWCC and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity functions. A physical modelling system involving TEROS probes and filter paper tests (FP) were used to derive the SWCC and fitting parameters using the van Genuchten (VG) and Fredlund and Xing (FX) models, and evaluate the conditional uncertainty of the fitting parameters and their propagation into unsaturated hydraulic conductivity using the restricted VG model. An important aspect of the study is advancing uncertainty assessment in the measurement of SWCC and its propagation into unsaturated hydraulic conductivity in ASD tropical residual soils. The study found that accounting for temporal dependence in TEROS measurements and in similar time-series SWCC techniques yields more representative uncertainty estimates for the Van Genuchten fitting parameters. Furthermore, it is found that the type of SWCC testing technique significantly affects the uncertainty of SWCC fitting parameters and their propagation into predicted unsaturated hydraulic conductivity. The study highlights the importance of accounting for soil structure, experimental configuration, and temporal measurement dependence when characterising unsaturated hydraulic behaviour, thereby improving the reliability of hydraulic parameters used in geotechnical analyses.

papers.title: Model test and numerical simulation study on large-scale caisson sinking based on hydraulic soil-breaking technology
papers.summary: During the penetration of large caissons into hard soil strata, conventional excavation methods often encounter difficulties in effectively reducing the excessive tip resistance developed beneath the cutting edge. Based on the soil erosion mechanism induced by high-pressure water jets, scaled model tests and numerical analyses were conducted to investigate hydraulic soil-breaking for caisson sinking. The effects of different jet pressures on soil removal around the cutting edge and the localized sinking response of the caisson were examined. A three-dimensional finite element model incorporating the impact and cutting effects of high-pressure water jets was developed to evaluate the influences of jet pressure and nozzle diameter on hydraulic soil-breaking performance. The numerical results were compared with experimental observations for validation. The results demonstrate that the numerical predictions agree well with the model test results, confirming the reliability of the proposed simulation method. After activating the hydraulic soil-breaking system, the caisson sinking displacement increased significantly, accompanied by a reduction in soil pressure beneath the cutting edge. Increasing the jet pressure and nozzle diameter further improved the sinking efficiency; however, it also aggravated the differential settlement of the caisson. Therefore, appropriate combinations of jet pressure and nozzle diameter should be selected in practical engineering applications to achieve a balance between penetration efficiency and construction stability. Since the model did not incorporate internal partition walls, the findings are mainly applicable to the analysis of localized hydraulic soil-breaking behavior and the reduction of cutting-edge resistance in the caisson wall–cutting edge zone.

papers.title: Resource-Efficient Laterite-Bentonite Barriers for Urban Waste Containment: Hydro-Chemo-Microstructural Controls on Suction Evolution
papers.summary: Sustainable urban development requires durable environmental containment infrastructure, such as systems in contaminated sites, barriers, and landfill liners, that are subjected to chemically variable pore fluids. Laterite–bentonite mixtures represent a potential resource-efficient barrier material, as small additions of bentonite can improve the water-retention properties of lateritic matrices. Yet, the interplay between bentonite content, dry density, and pore-fluid chemistry in controlling suction and microstructure remains poorly understood. The study focuses on compacted laterite-bentonite mixtures containing 3–7% bentonite, tested at dry densities of 1.5 and 1.6 g/cm³ in deionised water, NaCl, and CaCl₂. The filter paper method and WP4C were used to assess matric and total suction, respectively, while mercury intrusion porosimetry and scanning electron microscopy characterised pore-size distribution and microstructural evolution, respectively. The findings show a nonlinear suction response, with an approximate threshold of 5% bentonite coinciding with a change in the primary pore-structural response. Fluid pore chemistry affects water-retention characteristics, while pore constriction caused by increased dry density typically increases suction. Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ produce different microstructural responses, with Ca²⁺ favouring flocculation and aggregation, increasing macroporosity, and decreasing microporosity. The use of suction, MIP and SEM observations constitutes a hydro-chemo-microstructural relationship between ionic interactions and the evolution of suction and pore-size redistribution. The results offer a mechanistic understanding to optimise laterite-bentonite formulations for durable, resource-efficient environmental containment infrastructure.

papers.title: Relationship between thermal and electrical conductivity curves of soils with a unimodal pore size distribution: Part 2. Estimating bulk electrical conductivity from thermal conductivity
papers.summary: Soil thermal conductivity (λ) and electrical conductivity (σ) influence heat conduction and electrical conduction through soils. In Part 1 of this two-part series, we demonstrated that for soils with a unimodal pore size dis tribution, the λ and σ curves were interrelated and could be described with a unified series–parallel resistor model. Based on the conceptual model presented in Part 1, the “mirror image” phenomenon in the λ-σ rela tionship was further evaluated. Starting with the Lu et al. (2007) λ model, the “mirror image” phenomenon was used to derive a new normalized σ model. The new σ model was dependent on degree of water saturation (S), and shared the same shape parameters as those in the λ model. Here, the new σ model is examined using new datasets consisting of simultaneous thermo-TDR sensor measurements of soil water content (θ), λ and σ. New model σ values interpolated between known dry and saturated σ values agreed well with measured σ values, with RMSE values within 0.102 dS m1 and bias values between 0.083 and 0.014 dS m1 for a variety of soil samples. Using repeated in situ λ measurements made in soils during an evaporative drying period, the new σ model estimated normalized σ values with RMSEs within 0.015 dS m1. The new σ model offers an effective way to estimate σ of unsaturated soils.

papers.title: Relationships among hydraulic, thermal, and electrical properties of unsaturated soils
papers.summary: The water content, energy status, and hydraulic parameters are essential for studying the physical, chemical, and biological processes in unsaturated soils, and for improving agricultural production and managing ecological environment. We also explored the similarities of soil water flow, heat flow, and electric flow, and developed models for estimating SWRC.

Multi-method geophysical characterization and failure mechanism of a rainfall-induced loess landslide constrained by borehole data: a case study in Zichang, Yan’an
papers.summary: Abstract Background Rainfall-induced loess landslides threaten the Chinese Loess Plateau, yet their internal structure is hard to resolve because boreholes are point-wise and any single geophysical method is inherently non-unique. This study integrates electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), ground-penetrating radar (GPR), and shallow seismic reflection with 11 boreholes at the Shitaishan landslide (~10.3 × 10 4 m 3 , Zichang County, northern Shaanxi) to establish a borehole-constrained multi-method interpretation framework and elucidate its failure mechanism. Results Cross-validation among the three methods reveals a valley-dipping bedrock surface (~998 m at the toe, >1007 m at the rear). A laterally extensive low-resistivity zone (12–50 Ω·m) coinciding with suppressed radar amplitudes delineates an anomalous moisture accumulation zone in the frontal slide mass. A segmented sliding pattern is identified: the frontal block translated along the loess–bedrock contact, while the rear block failed along a moisture-softened interlayer within the loess sequence. Four coupled factors drove the failure: adverse bedrock topography providing a basal sliding surface, a low-permeability paleosol cap trapping infiltrated water, tension cracks funneling surface runoff into the slide body, and two episodes of heavy rainfall in June 2017. Each element is independently corroborated by at least two geophysical datasets or borehole logs. Conclusions Borehole-constrained multi-method geophysical interpretation effectively overcomes the non-uniqueness of single-method inversion and produces a high-confidence subsurface structural model. The segmented failure mode and four-factor coupling mechanism revealed here provide a transferable reference for landslide investigation and hazard mitigation in loess terrain.

Detail–Context Adaptive Structured Pruning Under Spatial Dependence for Multitemporal Landslide Segmentation
papers.summary: Landslide segmentation from multitemporal imagery must retain sparse scars and irregular boundaries. Efficient repeated mapping also requires models with manageable computation and storage. We use a 21-channel input design combining pre- and post-event reflectance, their differences, terrain and validity. We propose detail–context adaptive pruning (DCAP), which optimizes learnable channel scaling factors (gates) shared across dependency groups under a computation budget and recovers pruned models with task-aware losses. Evaluation uses model ensembles on 990 training, 132 validation and 198 test chips from Nepal in 2017–2019, separated by whole spatial groups. Under common task-aware recovery, the proposed method reduced multiply–accumulate operations (MACs) by 70.03% and parameters by 88.56%, while validation average precision (AP) and Dice increased from 0.4900/0.5154 to 0.4949/0.5238. On test, AP was 0.4268, a 0.65-percentage-point decrease, whereas Dice reached 0.4791, a 0.31-percentage-point increase. Joint bootstrap support was 1.0000 on validation. Small-component uncertainty limited DCAP’s test support to 0.9484, below the required 0.95; Group Taylor reached 85.11% MAC reduction under the validation rule, with test support 0.7933. Loss ablations showed endpoint-specific contributions and trade-offs. Geographic validation achieved 54.21% chip-weighted MAC reduction with inner-selected models, including dense fallback in the west. FP32 CUDA Graphs reduced DCAP latency by 34.1% on RTX 4080 and 32.5% on Jetson AGX Orin. These findings support substantial compression with small aggregate-score changes within the sampled population, while transfer to independent events has not been established.

papers.summary: Although marginal soils are increasingly used in MSE wall construction, calibrated pullout design parameters for such backfills remain limited. No prior studies have examined pullout behavior of lateritic soils under active rainfall infiltration to establish design reduction factors. This study presents a comprehensive large-scale pullout testing program to investigate the soil-geosynthetic interaction, particularly at the onset of rainfall infiltration. A custom pullout apparatus and rainfall simulator were developed. Pullout resistance of geogrids increased from 11 kN/m to 27.2 kN/m as the normal stress increased from 12.5 to 50 kN/m2. Based on tests on backfill soils from 22 locations, a reduction factor, Rf = 0.937e−0.02PI, is proposed for the pullout parameter F*α to account for moisture variation. In addition to conventional geogrids (GG), two composite reinforcements (CGR-1 and CGR-2) with drainage and reinforcement functions were also evaluated. CGR-2 exhibited 61.3% higher pullout capacity than CGR-1 due to greater skin friction and passive resistance. Under infiltration, interaction reduction was 66.3% for GG, compared to 19% and 14% for CGR-1 and CGR-2, respectively, indicating superior performance of composite reinforcements, particularly CGR-2, under rainfall conditions.

Stability Assessment of Landslides under Coupling Action of Rainfall and Earthquake
papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

papers.summary: Landslides are among the most common natural hazards in the hilly and mountainous regions of Jammu and Kashmir, India. The present study was conducted to assess the impacts of landslides across three selected sites in Doda district, Thathri, Kastigarh, and Pul Doda in 2026. Both primary and secondary data were collected during and after the monsoon season through field visits, direct observations, and structured questionnaire surveys administered to 151 respondents selected via purposive and random sampling techniques. Secondary data were compiled from peer-reviewed literature, government records, and official disaster reports. The study recorded 3 human fatalities and 18 injuries at Thathri, 1 fatality and 9 injuries at Kastigarh, and 0 fatalities and 13 injuries at Pul Doda. Respondents also reported extensive damage to residential houses, commercial shops, roads, vehicles, agricultural land, trees, and natural vegetation. Road blockages and transportation disruptions were the most widespread challenges across all three locations. Additionally, landslides contaminated local water sources, causing prolonged turbidity and water quality degradation. These findings demonstrate that landslides in Doda district generate severe socio-economic and environmental consequences. The results provide site-specific baseline evidence to support improved land-use planning, slope stabilization, road engineering and disaster risk reduction in the region. The study highlighted the need for effective landslide risk-reduction measures in Thathri, Kastigarh and Pul Doda. The slope should be stabilised through retaining walls, gabion structures, rock bolting and other suitable engineering techniques at vulnerable locations to reduce the future losses of life, property and environmental resources in Doda district.

Numerical Simulation of Landslide-Generated Waves in Reservoirs Using a Coupled SPH-DCDEM Method
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide-generated waves occur when sliding masses impact the water surface, potentially posing significant hazards to nearby areas. This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. The accuracy and effectiveness of the SPH-DCDEM method in simulating landslide-generated waves are validated using two physical model experiments of subaerial landslide-generated waves. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.summary: Abstract Mass movements such as landslides, lahars, and pyroclastic density currents pose substantial hazards, but can be difficult to locate when they occur in remote regions with limited visibility and/or overnight. These flows generate seismic and acoustic signals that are characterized by emergent onsets, making the location of events challenging. Amplitude‐based seismic methods address this problem by using the spatial pattern of amplitudes across a network rather than relying on arrival‐time picks. Here, we analyzed a suspected landslide signal recorded at Ngauruhoe, New Zealand, on 21 March 2026 using two amplitude‐based methods, Amplitude Source Location and Seismic Amplitude Ratio Analysis, together with a third method based on differential arrival times between seismic and infrasound waves. This is the first time all three localization methods have been compared, and they all placed the source on the eastern flank of the volcano. The amplitude‐based methods can be applied through time to track the evolving seismic source and are computationally efficient enough for real‐time use. These results show that both seismic amplitude methods and differential seismic‐infrasound arrival‐time methods can provide rapid first‐order localization of emergent mass‐movement signals for operational monitoring.

Integrating Geomorphological Controls into Landslide Susceptibility Mapping via Logistic Regression: A Case Study of the Nam San Sub-Watershed, Loei Province, Thailand
papers.summary: Landslide disasters in the Nam San sub-watershed cause ongoing damage to lives and property. This study aims to evaluate landslide susceptibility by applying geo-information technology combined with logistic regression analysis in the Nam San sub-watershed, Loei Province, Thailand. The 16 variables used included: elevation, slope, geology, soil permeability, distance to stream, topographic wetness index (TWI), stream power index (SPI), sediment transport index (STI), topographic roughness index (TRI), drainage density (DD), stream frequency (SF), infiltration number (IN), mean annual precipitation, distance to road, distance to village, and land use. The study found that hydrogeological variables, particularly the STI, TRI, and DD, had the greatest influence on the risk assessment model, effectively reflecting the erosion and water accumulation mechanisms at the sub-watershed level. The newly developed landslide risk map can classify risk into five levels as follows: very high-risk area (29.17 km2, 3.43%), high risk area (229.35 km2, 26.94%), medium risk area (305.74 km2, 35.91%), Low risk area (267.02 km2, 31.36%), and very low risk area (20.17 km2, 2.37%). When comparing the accuracy of landslide sites with actual historical landslide fault locations (1989–2026), the results revealed that the vast majority of historical landslides fell within the high and very high susceptibility zones. Specifically, 35 landslide events (17.76%) were located in very high-risk areas, and 85 events (43.15%) occurred in high-risk areas. These high-susceptibility zones were predominantly concentrated along foothills and undulating central plains, particularly where hillsides had been excavated for road construction and converted into monoculture farming. This study provides a highly accurate geo-information tool for use as a database to support effective disaster management planning and local land use management.

Static and Dynamic Responses of a Valley-Type Ash Storage Dam After Intense Rainfall
papers.summary: This study examined the effects of post-rainfall hydrological conditions on the stability and seismic response of a valley-type ash storage dam in Liaoning, China. Laboratory tests and field water-level measurements were combined with sequential seepage, static stability, and dynamic analyses. The mean absolute error between the calculated and measured water levels at four monitoring points was 0.565 m. Dynamic triaxial tests revealed a decrease in the shear modulus ratio and an increase in the damping ratio with increasing effective shear strain. After receiving a uniform rainfall of 96 mm/d for 48 h, the dry beach length decreased from 100 to 50 m; for the same cumulative rainfall and duration, a late-peaking pattern reduced it to 30 m. The static factor of safety of the starter dam decreased by approximately 20%. At input amplitudes of 0.125 and 0.200 g, the relative acceleration and total displacement increased after rainfall. The largest local responses were observed near the crest and upper slope, and the starter dam had a lower factor of safety. These results indicate distinct spatial patterns of sliding stability and local seismic response for the modeled dam.

Analytical Solutions for Water Infiltration in an Infinite Vegetated Slope under Heavy Rainfall and Its Shallow Stability
papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

Impact of Rainfall Infiltration on Groundwater Seepage under the Effect of Urban Construction in Shanghai
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater seepage is influenced by various anthropogenic factors during urban construction, among which subsurface structures and surface hardening are two key factors. This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

papers.summary: Based on the theory of thermoelastic wave propagation, a dynamic analysis model of a bedrock-saturated soil-layered unsaturated soil site under S-wave incidence is established in this paper. Using the transfer matrix method, combined with the boundary conditions, the recursive relationship of the amplitude vector between the media layers is established, and the influence of the thermal-hydro-mechanical multi-field coupling on the seismic response of the site is systematically studied. The findings indicate that the vertical displacement amplification coefficient of the site is, in general, greater than that of the horizontal direction, with a maximum ratio of up to 36.04, and the peak value mostly occurs at incident angles less than [Formula: see text]. The soil structure has a significant effect on the propagation of seismic waves: Case 1 (homogeneous) displacement response is gentle; Case 2 (upper soft and lower stiff) fluctuates markedly at incident angles of less than [Formula: see text]; and Case 3 (upper stiff and lower soft) is relatively stable. The parameter sensitivity analysis shows that the change in groundwater level [Formula: see text] has the most significant influence on the displacement response, followed by the phase delay time of heat flux [Formula: see text] and the thickness of the first layer of unsaturated soil [Formula: see text], while the influence of Kelvin medium temperature [Formula: see text] and thermal conductivity [Formula: see text] is relatively limited. It shows that the amplification effect of soil conditions and the thermodynamic environment on seismic response is much higher than that of thermal conductivity. In engineering practice, systematic and coordinated measurement and comprehensive analysis of soil physical parameters should be carried out to effectively control the risk of structural damage under earthquake action.

Closed-Form Solutions for Temperature-Dependent Suction Stress under Transient Infiltration in Unsaturated Soil: An Application for Stability Analysis of Strip Plate Anchors
papers.summary: Abstract The soil layer up to a certain depth below the ground surface exists in an unsaturated state, where factors such as precipitation, evaporation, and prolonged subsurface heat waves control the state and material properties of soil. The suction stress that contributes to the resistance of the soil mass governs the stability of geostructures and depends on the thermal and hydraulic interactions in unsaturated soil. No solutions are available to determine the suction stress in soils subjected to transient flow conditions at elevated temperatures. This study develops closed-form expressions for temperature-dependent suction stress under transient flow conditions using the one-dimensional transient flow equation and a temperature-dependent soil–water retention curve. The developed equation was implemented within the framework of stress-based finite-element limit analysis to evaluate the stability of strip plate anchors in terms of their uplift capacity embedded in unsaturated sand, silt, and clay under transient flow conditions and varying temperatures. The critical role of thermal and hydraulic interactions in different types of unsaturated soils (clay, silt, and sand), specifically regarding matric suction, effective degree of saturation, and suction stress over time, has been discussed in detail. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

Soil–foundation–structure interaction in bridges with rocking foundations on unsaturated soil layers
papers.summary: Rocking foundations are increasingly used in bridge design, yet their seismic performance under unsaturated soil conditions remains poorly understood. In this study, dynamic centrifuge experiments are used to investigate the seismic response of a single-span bridge with rocking shallow foundations resting on soils with different saturation states. Tests were conducted under dry, fully saturated and partially saturated conditions with varying water table depths and multiple earthquake input motions. The objectives are to evaluate the influence of the water table level on rocking behaviour and system response, examine the interaction between soil saturation and seismic motion characteristics, and assess the applicability of simplified single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) representations for bridge systems. The results show that water table depth has a pronounced effect on a foundation’s rocking response and overall bridge behaviour, influencing deformation demands, system stiffness, damping and mobilised overturning moments. Unsaturated conditions generally reduce residual deformations while increasing foundation moment demand. Comparisons with SDOF models reveal systematic differences in moment capacity, indicating that direct transfer of SDOF-based results to bridge systems may lead to biased moment capacity estimates due to axial load redistribution imposed by deck constraints. Based on experimental observations, a correction approach is proposed to improve moment capacity estimation for rocking bridge foundations on unsaturated soils.

Vertical Acceleration Effect on Slope Stability: A Simplified Coupled Insight
papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

papers.summary: Limit-equilibrium analysis is the usual way to assess the stability of a slope through its factor of safety (FOS). This Data Descriptor presents 43,637 analyses of homogeneous, drained slopes with no water table or external load, solved with the Bishop simplified method on circular surfaces. Each analysis maps five geometric and soil parameters to the FOS, the critical circle and the search diagnostics. The contribution is the open curation and benchmarking of these data, not a new stability method. The analyses were generated for a study of sampling strategies for surrogate models and first deposited with that study; they are reorganized here for reuse without changing a stored value, and the quality checks are given in added columns. Three linked tables give the distinct analyses, their place in the source deposit, and fixed benchmark splits: 22,000 uniformly drawn analyses for training, three disjoint test sets, and a grouped split that holds out regions of the dimensionless space. Boundary cases were solved again on enlarged domains, non-converged searches were rerun to convergence, and 15 analyses were compared blind with Slide2, agreeing within 0.6% in 14 cases. Random-forest and nearest-neighbor baselines are given for reference.

papers.summary: Abstract In this study, a hydraulic-mechanical coupled model of unsaturated soil considering the effect of time was established based on unsaturated elastic-plastic theory. The model considers not only the influence of the degree of saturation and viscoplastic strain on soil hardening but also that of viscous volumetric strain on the soil-water characteristic curve. The model could completely describe creep, soil-water characteristics, and mechanical properties of unsaturated soil. The elastic-viscoplastic uniform tangent modulus of the coupled model was derived using an implicit integration algorithm. The user material ( U mat ) subroutine was written using the algorithm so that the tangent stiffness matrix could be exported for finite-element calculations. To validate the correctness of the algorithm and program, the model parameters were obtained from wetting-drying cycles and isotropic compression tests. The program was used to predict creep, mechanical, and hydraulic properties under shearing creep and triaxial compression tests. Comparison of the predictions with the experimental results indicated that the coupled model was able to capture the main features of time-dependent hydraulic-mechanical coupled behavior, including hydraulic and mechanical behavior.

papers.summary: Abstract Probabilistic stability analysis of soil slopes is essential for reliable geotechnical design due to pronounced uncertainties in soil strength and hydraulic parameters. Although crude Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) provides a robust benchmark, its prohibitive computational cost and the limitations of gradient-based methods such as FORM and SORM in handling nonlinear and non-Gaussian performance functions restrict their practical applicability. To address these challenges, this study conducts a comparative analysis of advanced surrogate-based reliability methods, specifically polynomial chaos expansion–enhanced Monte Carlo simulation (PCE-MCS) and kriging-enhanced Monte Carlo simulation (K-MCS), against traditional gradient-based methods such as the first-order reliability method (FORM) and second-order reliability method (SORM) for evaluating the stability of unsaturated finite soil slopes. The crude MCS serves as the benchmark. The work examines the predictive accuracy and computational efficiency of these methods in estimating the probability of failure ( p f ). Parametric studies demonstrate nonlinear variations in p f with mean and coefficient of variation of stability number ( c / γ H ), internal friction angle ( ϕ ), and fitting parameters of soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC) ( a f / γ H , n f , and m f ). In terms of computational efficiency, surrogate-assisted approaches provide orders-of-magnitude reductions in wall-clock time compared to crude MCS. When normalized with respect to PCE-MCS (unity), K-MCS requires only 1.85 times the computational cost, whereas FORM/SORM requires approximately 28 times. In contrast, crude MCS incurs computational costs exceeding four orders of magnitude for large sample sizes. Statistical testing confirms that stochastic methods (K-MCS, PCE-MCS) significantly outperformed gradient-based methods (FORM, SORM). papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most significant natural hazards in the Himalayan region of India, causing substantial damage to infrastructure, natural resources, and local communities. This study presents an integrated hydro-geotechnical approach for regional landslide susceptibility assessment by combining statistical susceptibility mapping with slope stability evaluation. The proposed framework considers the influence of key hydrologic factors, including rainfall, drainage density, topographic wetness, and groundwater conditions, together with geotechnical properties to better explain the mechanisms controlling slope failure. Five bivariate statistical models, namely, frequency ratio (FR), information value (IV), weight of evidence (WoE), certainty factor (CF), and Shannon entropy (SE), were applied to produce landslide susceptibility maps. Their performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) and landslide density index (LDI). Among the evaluated models, SE achieved the highest predictive accuracy ( AUC = 87.17 % ), followed closely by FR (87.06%). The results indicate that steep slopes ( > 30 ° ), weak lithological formations, high drainage density, and groundwater conditions are the main factors controlling landslide occurrence in the study area. Slope stability was further evaluated using laboratory-derived geotechnical parameters and circular failure charts (CFC), providing an independent assessment of slope conditions under different groundwater scenarios. The combined use of statistical modeling, hydrologic factors, and geotechnical verification improves the reliability of landslide susceptibility assessment and provides a practical framework that can be applied in other mountainous regions affected by rainfall-induced landslides.

The literature is examined with emphasis on its relevance to the engineering characteristics, instability mechanisms, reinforcement technologies, and monitoring methods of these soils. A thematic comparative approach is adopted to synthesize findings from experimental investigations, numerical simulations, and field studies, with particular attention to hydro-mechanical interactions and engineering applicability. The instability mechanisms of special soils under heavy rainfall and hydro-mechanical coupling effects are analyzed, identifying the underlying mechanisms that induce non-uniform subgrade settlement and early distresses in upper pavement structures. Meanwhile, the evolution trends of reinforcement and monitoring technologies for special soils are reviewed. Soil stabilization techniques have increasingly incorporated industrial wastes and biomaterials, such as steel slag and lignin, which effectively enhance soil water stability and resistance to permanent deformation under cyclic loading. Concurrently, intelligent monitoring relies on the Internet of Things (IoT) sensing and data-driven algorithms to achieve dynamic and quantitative risk early warning. Finally, prospective research directions are identified, including long-term service performance under extreme environments, the development of advanced constitutive models under multi-field coupling, and the construction of intelligent collaborative control systems for subgrade-pavement structures. papers.summary: Flooding, soil erosion, and sediment transport are interconnected environmental and socio-economic challenges in Rwanda, particularly in the Nyabarongo Catchment, where steep terrain, intense rainfall, land-use change, urbanisation, deforestation, and mining intensify runoff, erosion, and sediment delivery. This thesis investigates how institutional flood risk management, spatial risk assessment, and Naturebased Solutions (NbS) can be integrated to support evidence-based flood and sediment management. Four complementary studies examine institutional flood risk management, flood susceptibility, soil erosion susceptibility, and NbS planning and implementation. The institutional assessment identifies fragmented data management, limited technical capacity, and governance based largely on administrative rather than hydrological boundaries, highlighting the need for proactive catchment-based management. GIS, remote sensing, machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and spatial analysis were used to assess flood and erosion susceptibility. Random Forest achieved the highest flood prediction performance (AUC = 0.968; F1-score = 0.92), with 15.6% of the catchment classified as highly to very highly susceptible. For soil erosion, CatBoost achieved an AUC of 0.974 and F1-score of 0.91, with approximately half of the catchment classified as moderately to very highly susceptible. Stakeholder and documentary evidence indicate widespread implementation and perceived benefits of NbS, but limited monitoring, technical and financial constraints, fragmented coordination, and maintenance challenges hinder evaluation of their long-term effectiveness. The thesis proposes an integrated framework linking spatial assessment, site-specific NbS selection, field validation, continuous monitoring, stakeholder participation, adaptive governance, and evidence-based scaling, offering transferable insights for other data-constrained tropical catchments.

papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Muhammadiyah Surakarta)
authors: , Dr. Annisa Trisnia Sasmi, S.Si., M.T
papers.summary: Gedangsari District, Gunungkidul Regency, is an area with potential landslide susceptibility due to its physical characteristics, which are influenced by slope gradient, rainfall, rock types, soil types, and land use. This study aims to (1) map landslide susceptibility levels in Gedangsari District, Gunungkidul Regency, and (2) determine priority areas for mitigation based on landslide susceptibility levels. The analysis was conducted using a Geographic Information System (GIS) with spatial data comprising slope gradient, rainfall, rock types, soil types, and land use. The data were processed using the Weighted Overlay method with the assistance of ArcGIS Pro software. The results show that the study area is predominantly classified as having high landslide susceptibility, covering 37.303 km² or 55.25% of the total area. The moderate susceptibility class covers 30.085 km² or 44.56%, while the low susceptibility class covers 0.125 km² or 0.19%. Based on this classification, areas with high susceptibility are designated as Priority I, areas with moderate susceptibility as Priority II, and areas with low susceptibility as Priority III. The predominance of the high susceptibility class indicates that most of the areas identified through the classification require attention in landslide mitigation efforts. The resulting susceptibility map is expected to serve as a source of spatial information and a reference for regional planning and the determination of landslide mitigation priorities in Gedangsari District, Gunungkidul Regency.

papers.title: Analisis Kerawanan dan Probabilitas Longsor di Kecamatan Sawangan Kabupaten Magelang
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Muhammadiyah Surakarta)
papers.summary: Sawangan District in Magelang Regency is an area prone to landslides due to topographic conditions and environmental characteristics that facilitate their occurrence. Situated between Mount Merapi and Mount Merbabu, the region features varying slope gradients, unconsolidated volcanic materials, and relatively high rainfall. This study aims to analyze landslide susceptibility levels for 2025 and the probability of landslide occurrence in Sawangan District during the 2024–2025 period. A descriptivequantitative method was employed, utilizing a spatial analysis approach specifically overlay and scoring techniques alongside binary logistic regression analysis to determine landslide probability values. Sampling was conducted using a purposive sampling method based on five environmental parameters and recorded landslide locations. The research results indicate that Sawangan District is categorized into four landslide susceptibility classes: not susceptible, slightly susceptible, susceptible, and highly susceptible. Binary logistic regression analysis reveals that landslide probability falls into four classes low, moderate, high, and very high, with an AUC value of 0.846, demonstrating the model's good discriminative ability in distinguishing between landslide and non-landslide locations. While landslide occurrences are predominantly found in the susceptible and highly susceptible classes, some incidents also occurred in the slightly susceptible and not susceptible classes. These findings indicate that landslides can occur across various levels of susceptibility and slope gradients; therefore, vigilance is required not only in areas with high susceptibility but also in those with lower susceptibility. Overlay analysis reveals a link between susceptibility and landslide probability, though the two do not always exhibit a direct, consistent relationship

papers.summary: The conversion of forest land to agricultural land can alter vegetation cover and affect slope stability. This study aims to identify changes in land cover and map landslide risk levels in Kempo Subdistrict, Dompu Regency. The study employed a descriptive quantitative approach based on Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Secondary data used included land cover, rainfall, slope gradient, soil type, and administrative boundaries. Analysis was conducted through classification, scoring, weighting, and parameter overlay using QGIS. The results of the study show changes in land cover during the observation period, particularly an increase in the area of dryland agriculture from 7,594.37 ha in 2017 to 9,729.13 ha in 2021, while scrubland decreased from 3,029.54 ha to 1,382.39 ha. Landslide risk mapping identified three classes: low, moderate, and high. High-risk zones are primarily associated with hilly areas, steep to very steep slopes, Lithosol soils, relatively high rainfall, and land cover that has been converted to agricultural or open land. These results can serve as supporting information for land management and landslide mitigation in Kempo Subdistrict. Field validation and data alignment are necessary to improve the accuracy of the results.

papers.title: Numerical and experimental investigation of medium density polyethylene pipes under lateral ground movements
papers.summary: Buried pipelines are a critical component of infrastructure networks transporting water, wastewater, oil, and natural gas over long distances. The pipes are sometimes exposed to geotechnical hazards such as landslides, ground settlement, and liquefaction-induced lateral spreading, which can affect the structural integrity of these assets. Proper estimation of the induced stress or strain due to such geohazards is an important engineering consideration for safe and economic design of pipelines. Current pipe design guidelines recommend the beam-on-spring model for assessing pipeline distress caused by ground movements. The guidelines provide spring models developed from studies using steel pipe segments. The applicability of the recommendations for flexible medium-density polyethylene pipes, commonly used in gas distribution systems, was not evaluated due to a lack of controlled experimental data. The primary objective of the current study is to develop an experimental database, evaluate current design recommendations, and improve the understanding of soil–pipe interaction behaviour for flexible medium-density polyethylene (MDPE) pipelines subjected to lateral ground movement. The tests were conducted on 42.2-mm and 60.3-mm diameter pipes buried at various embedment ratios. Because some critical responses, such as localized force-displacement responses, could not be measured during the experiment, a three-dimensional finite element (3D FE) model was developed to simulate test results from the literature and those from the current study. The 3D FE model was then used to examine the pipe–soil interaction for pipes with different flexural rigidity. The results of the 3D FE analysis were suitable for critically examining the localized load-displacement responses to evaluate the spring models. papers.title: Landslide Dams Triggered by Extreme Rainfall Events: A Tairāwhiti Gisborne Case Study
papers.source: Open Access Victoria University of Wellington | Te Herenga Waka (Figshare)
papers.summary: Landslide dams, formed when landslide debris blocks a river, occur across Aotearoa New Zealand. These events pose serious hazards to downstream communities and infrastructure, as sudden breaches can result in unexpected flooding and debris flows. They are also important components of complex cascading slope-river systems. Despite their contribution to sediment cascades and potential flood hazard, they remain under-researched. Understanding the interactions between hydrological, geological, and climatic factors governing landslide dam evolution is crucial for hazard management planning. The Tairāwhiti Gisborne region on the East Coast of Aotearoa New Zealand is prone to landslides and subsequent dams, due to its steep slopes, susceptible lithology, and exposure to tropical storms from the east. Despite this vulnerability, very little is known about the material properties and behaviour of landslide dams in this area. The primary aim of this thesis was to investigate the geomorphic and geotechnical aspects of dams in the Tairāwhiti Gisborne region, to understand their formation and breach processes. Two large landslide dams were chosen as case studies, the 1,485,500 m3 Waiorongomai Landslide Dam which formed in the north of the region in early January 2023, and the 98,500 m3 Tiniroto Landslide Dam which formed in the south of the region on the 3rd of October 2023. Three elements of analyses were used to investigate these landslide dams. First, historic landslides were mapped in the two catchments, to investigate the rate of landslide-river connectivity and landslide dam frequency. Each landslide source and deposit were mapped as polygons, using aerial imagery between 1988 and 2023. Second, the short-term evolution of the Waiorongomai and Tiniroto landslide dams was documented through a series of engineering geomorphic maps, using LiDAR and aerial imagery in ArcGIS Pro. Finally, the grain size distribution, liquid and plastic limits, and slake durability were analysed

papers.summary: Rainfall-induced shallow landslides are rapid slope failures within shallow soil layers, generally less than 2 m thick, that are triggered by intense or prolonged rainfall on steep soilmantled slopes.NASA's Global Landslide Catalog recorded 11,033 reported rainfall-triggered landslides during 2007-2019, and an overlay with the FAO land-cover map indicated that up to 80% occurred in vegetated land-cover types.These observations show that vegetation does not uniformly prevent landslides.Its stabilizing effect has conventionally been represented mainly as additional root cohesion, although rainfall-induced instability is controlled by interactions among precipitation, hydrological responses, root-system architecture, soil depth, and the potential failure zone.Roots can increase mechanical resistance while also modifying infiltration, preferential flow, runoff, soil-water redistribution, saturation, and pore-waterpressure development.Consequently, the same root system can reinforce shallow soil but promote hydrological weakening where water is transferred beneath the principal rooting zone.

papers.summary: The main purpose of this thesis is on one hand to enhance the current predictive capabilities of the stability of soil slopes and on the other hand, to improve the design practice to stabilise natural slopes showing signs of distress and make the design of engineered slopes more affordable. To achieve the first objective an analytical method achieved by the upper bound theorem of limit analysis and the pseudo-static approach is derived for the assessment of the stability of slopes manifesting vertical cracks and subject to seismic action. The method is validated by numerical limit analyses and displacement-based finite-element analyses with strength reduction technique. Employing this method slope stability charts to assess the stability factor for fissured slopes subject to both horizontal and vertical accelerations for any combination of c, φ, and slope inclination are produced. To achieve the second objective limit analysis was employed to derive a semi-analytical method to extend the applicability of current method to design the slope reinforcement for frictional backfills to cohesive frictional backfills. Design charts providing the amount of reinforcement needed as a function of cohesion, tensile strength, angle of shearing resistance and slope inclination are obtained. From the results, it emerges that accounting for the presence of cohesion allows significant savings to be made, and that cracks are often significantly detrimental to slope stability so they cannot be overlooked in the design calculations of the reinforcement. Also, a new numerical method to determine multi-linear profiles of optimal shapes for reinforced slopes in frictional backfills is presented. papers.source: UPCommons institutional repository (Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)
papers.summary: Regional Landslide Early Warning Systems (LEWS) are essential tools for predicting rainfall-induced slope instability across broad geographic regions. This thesis provides an evaluation of the regional LEWS in Catalonia, Spain, assessing its real-time operational performance and sensitivity across operational factors (2024–2025) and its forecast reliability across 24 h and 48 h predictive lead times (2024–2026). The system inputs include precipitation datasets, Quantitative Precipitation Estimates (QPE) and Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPF), alongside a regional static susceptibility map and an official reported landslide inventory The evaluation framework applies an adapted Event-Duration Matrix (EDuMaP) methodology combined with spatial-fuzzy verification across slope units, municipalities, and counties. Real-time evaluations against reported landslide inventories showed that applying quality-control data filtering and a 48 h fuzzy verification window significantly improved system Hit Rates, confirming that inventory timing uncertainties often mask successful alerts. Factor sensitivity and multi-factor clustering revealed that during that while the real-time forecasting the system captures medium-to-large shallow slides and debris flows during intense convective storms (𝐼𝑒𝑞 higher than 50 mm/h, detecting 80–85% of events), structural blind spots exist. Current operational triggers miss slope failures driven by low-to-moderate rainfall (𝐼𝑒𝑞 lower than 30 mm/h) due to fixed 24 h accumulation windows that ignore antecedent rainfall and soil moisture, fine-scale road-cut failures smoothed out by 30 m DEM resolution, and lowsusceptibility mapped zones. Evaluating forecast reliability across 24 h and 48 h lead times revealed that performance drops substantially as lead times extend, with 𝐻𝑅𝑊 decreasing to ~25% and 𝑃𝑃𝑊falling to 36.0–50.0% at 48 h.
